questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for an Internal Developer Platform Team (Questions 46–60)

Streaming, since only streaming supports concurrency.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to run more than one request at a time.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: Most report sections are short, templated commentary (e.g., a routine "expense summary") generated at high volume with simple structure. Latency and cost matter far more than handling rare, highly complex sections well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every section.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity sections, reserving a higher tier only for sections flagged as complex.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the firm's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity sections fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator (Questions 31–45)

questions.prompt: A small fraction of report sections require tracing a multi-entity intercompany reconciliation, where the fast default model produces shallow, incomplete commentary. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

Switch every section to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Route only the flagged complex sections to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Increase max_tokens for all sections.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex sections to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B accepts avoidable risk; A and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

Lower the temperature to zero.
Ask the model to restate the structure before writing the report.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.

Output length has no effect on latency.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long input leaves less room for a long output, and vice versa.

Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. B, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per report, rather than an estimate from average length.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on transaction-row count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per report gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (A, C, D) don't.

Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.

Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole period."
Alphabetize the transactions before summarizing.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-figures summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; C and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., stated balances) against the source ledger rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Shorten the report so there's less room for errors.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source ledger catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and D don't address correctness.

Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main drafting step.

The choice has no effect on cost or latency.
For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.

Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.
Only allowing one designated analyst to ever read the prompt.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. B, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: A new engineer clones Arbor's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.

The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer using the Claude Agent SDK. It handles order-fulfillment exceptions — backorders, address problems, damaged-item claims, and refund requests — using custom tools (`check_inventory`, `create_shipping_label`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`). Refunds and label creation carry real financial and operational cost, so tool access and enforcement matter as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent calls `create_shipping_label` and `issue_refund` tools within a single turn. What should the orchestration code key off to know whether to keep executing tool calls and feeding results back, versus finishing the turn?

choices.text: Whether the agent's text includes phrases like "order resolved."
A hard limit of 5 tool calls per order.
Whether the last tool call succeeded without errors.
The `stop_reason` value returned with the response: keep looping while it is `"tool_use"`, stop when it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; tool errors (C) don't indicate loop completion.

The main agent orchestrates subagents — a company-researcher, a contacts-finder, and a competitive-analyst — and has tools including `search_web`, `get_crm_record`, `enrich_contact`, and `log_research_note`.
questions.prompt: Meridian is deciding between running the research agent through a hosted, Anthropic-managed execution environment versus self-hosting the harness on their own infrastructure. Question: What is the core tradeoff? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Operational control (self-hosted) versus operational burden (managed) — the tools the agent can call don't differ by deployment model.
Self-hosted agents cannot call custom tools like `enrich_contact`.
Managed agents are inherently less secure than self-hosted ones.
Managed agents cannot reach a company's internal CRM at all.

questions.explanation: The tradeoff is operational control versus operational burden; tool-calling capability doesn't differ between the two deployment models. B, C, and D are unsupported absolute claims.

choices.text: Whether the task uses more than three tools.
Whether the team prefers Python or TypeScript.
Whether the task must finish in under a minute.
Whether the task is well-defined and repeatable, versus high-ambiguity with a path that depends on intermediate findings.

questions.explanation: Task predictability versus dependency on intermediate results is the deciding factor between workflow and agent patterns, not language, tool count, or runtime.

questions.explanation: Subagent descriptions drive delegation choices; a vague description causes under-delegation regardless of how many tools the subagent has. B, C, and D misdiagnose the cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Fernbridge Marketplace lets sellers upload raw product listings — title, bullet points, sometimes a photo — in bulk. Claude enriches each listing into structured attributes (category, material, dimensions, safety flags) used for search and filtering. The pipeline handles both an interactive single-listing flow (a seller uploads one item and waits) and a nightly batch flow (hundreds of thousands of listings).
questions.prompt: The nightly batch job enriches 200,000 listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs a tool call mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model to reduce cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't support system prompts.
The 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic impossible.
The Batch API's context window is too small for long listings.
The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed results back to the model within a single request — required for this iterative loop.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and C misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Codeforge runs an internal code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across a large monorepo, summarizing changes, flagging risks, and suggesting fixes. It runs on every PR, so cost and latency matter, but a small fraction of PRs are complex refactors that need deeper reasoning.
questions.prompt: Most PRs are small and reviewable with straightforward checks; latency and cost per PR matter far more than handling rare, highly complex refactors well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity review, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every PR.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the hardest architectural reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. B and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every PR.
Route only the flagged complex PRs to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every PR to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all PRs.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or placed first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; diff-specific content should come after as the varying part.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average size or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the CI logs with a second Claude call before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. C and D work around the symptom without reducing waste; B adds cost without addressing the root problem.

questions.prompt: For very long PR diffs, reviewers notice the assistant consistently misses issues in the middle of the diff while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole diff."
Alphabetize the files before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear file headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. Shorten the review so there's less room for errors.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the actual diff catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

questions.prompt: A new data engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.

The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, C, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.

Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Locke LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, is deploying a contract-review agent to help attorneys review vendor contracts, NDAs, and lease agreements. The agent has tools including `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `redline_suggest`, and `request_attorney_review`. Because incorrect redlines or missed risk flags carry real legal and financial consequences, tool design and escalation policy matter as much as review quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants the contract-review agent's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until Claude has no more tool calls to make. What should the loop key off?

choices.text: Whether the redline text contains the phrase "no further changes."
The `stop_reason` field on each response: continue looping while it is `"tool_use"`, stop when it is `"end_turn"`.
A hard cap of five tool calls per contract.
Whether `flag_risk` returned any flags.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (C) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; whether flags were found (D) doesn't indicate loop completion.

questions.prompt: After `flag_risk` executes and returns identified risk clauses, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the contract?

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the tool_use ID to the conversation, then send the full conversation back to the model.
Store the flags in a separate risk database only, without returning them to the model.
Insert the flags into the system prompt so they persist for the rest of the review.
Start a new session summarizing the flags found so far.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: A post thread is very long (reply chains with 100+ comments), and the team wants a maximally detailed moderation report per comment, considering a very long requested output. What tradeoff must they account for?

choices.text: Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a long input thread leaves less room for a long output, and vice versa.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.
Output length has no effect on latency.
Input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long input thread directly constrains available output length and vice versa. B, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The moderation prompt currently places the specific post text before the general policy instructions and desired label format in every request. Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability?

Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Stable, role-defining policy instructions belong first (system prompt or first block) so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; post-specific content should come after as the varying part.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

Wall-clock latency per post, used as a cost proxy.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on post character count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per post gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

Prune the metadata to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before classifying.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.prompt: For very long comment threads, the team notices moderation misses violations in the middle of the thread while catching issues in the opening and closing comments well. What is the most effective mitigation?

Alphabetize the comments before classifying.

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.

Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.

Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main moderation step.

Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new QA engineer clones the team's test-automation repo, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established test-naming and assertion conventions, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new engineer cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to triage failing test runs and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The test runs are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.prompt: A downstream dashboard parses Claude Code's test-triage output with regex to auto-file defect tickets, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the triage-findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-parsing requirement.

questions.prompt: The team's `/scan-flaky-tests` custom command prints thousands of lines of historical test-run data, and testers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so testers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C restricts capability, not output destination; D removes useful functionality.

questions.prompt: An internal `/generate-test-fixtures` skill is meant only to create new fixture files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated config files. What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require testers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; B mitigates damage rather than preventing it; C is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: A QA engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar test-automation framework's fixture system works before writing new tests, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read every file in the framework in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; C doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the new tests in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a test-config file, calls an internal MCP tool to fetch environment status, and writes a defect-triage report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and B re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: A test-environment provisioning tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A and B guess without diagnosis; C doesn't investigate the cause at all.

Have each team paste defect-tracker API credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code defect-tracking logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the defect-tracker API manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. B, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
A Claude Code Skill.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether an internal MCP server for test-environment provisioning should run as a local stdio process per QA engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. What should drive the decision?

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and C are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a defect-tracker API token hardcoded directly in the file. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${DEFECT_TRACKER_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full test-suite deletion rights) than any actual QA workflow requires. What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and D are detective/compensating controls; B accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific test-report-formatting workflow used by a single small QA squad, versus a widely-reused environment-health-check capability needed by every agent across the org. How should each be built?

choices.text: The one-off report-formatting workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused environment-health-check capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. B, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 5.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Incident-Response Ops Agent for a Cloud Hosting Provider (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Kestrel Cloud runs virtual-machine and container hosting for mid-market customers. Its SRE team is building "Warden," an on-call assistant built on the Claude Agent SDK with custom tools (`check_node_health`, `restart_container`, `rotate_api_key`, `notify_customer`, `page_sre`). Warden triages incidents overnight before a human ever looks at them, so tool-execution correctness and guardrails matter as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: Warden's harness needs to know when to keep feeding tool results back to the model versus when the model is finished responding for the turn. Question: What should the harness check? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether the assistant's text includes phrases like "incident resolved."
A hardcoded limit of eight tool calls per session.
Whether `notify_customer` has been called yet.
The `stop_reason` on the response: keep looping while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text keywords (A) are unreliable, a call-count cap (B) is only a backstop, and waiting on a specific tool (C) doesn't reflect turn completion generally.

Warden triages incidents overnight before a human ever looks at them, so tool-execution correctness and guardrails matter as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: After Warden calls `rotate_api_key` and the harness executes it, what is required for Warden to reason correctly about the outcome on its next turn?

choices.text: Log the rotation to the audit database and let the next prompt reference it by ticket number.
Summarize the rotation result in a fresh system prompt for a new session.
Append the rotated key's confirmation to the end of the system prompt so it persists.
Add a `tool_result` block keyed to the original `tool_use` ID into the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be attached as a `tool_result` block referencing the original `tool_use` ID and the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate it. Logging elsewhere (A) keeps the result out of the model's reasoning; C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data; D-as-new-session (labeled B here) discards useful state unnecessarily.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.

questions.prompt: The orchestrator agent calls `lookup_company`, receives results, and must decide whether to call another tool or finish. What should the surrounding harness key off to know when to stop feeding tool results back into the loop?

choices.text: Whether the response text contains a phrase like "brief complete."
The `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools and returning results while it is `"tool_use"`, stop once it is `"end_turn"`.
A fixed cap of five tool calls per prospect, regardless of outcome.
Whether `lookup_company` returned a non-empty payload.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text phrases (A) are unreliable, a fixed cap (C) is a backstop rather than the primary signal, and a non-empty payload (D) doesn't indicate the model is done reasoning.

choices.text: The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — which this iterative loop requires.
The Batch API's 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic impossible to schedule.
The Batch API doesn't support system prompts, so validation instructions would be dropped.
The Batch API's context window is too small for a full product description.

questions.prompt: Most pull requests are small, routine changes (dependency bumps, formatting, minor refactors) where review is simple and extremely high-volume. choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee nothing is ever missed.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token, regardless of review quality on flagged diffs.
The same tier used for the team's hardest architectural reviews, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity diffs, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as higher-risk.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity PRs fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged higher-risk cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and C overspend by default; B ignores review-quality fit entirely.

Switch every PR to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Add many more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every PR.
Increase max_tokens for all PRs so comments can be longer.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged high-risk PRs to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume routine path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.

Wall-clock review latency per PR, used as a cost proxy.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from diff size or unrelated proxies (A, B, C) don't.

Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent drop in comment quality. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.
Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.

Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A frees trivial space while losing standards; B describes behavior that doesn't exist; C discards findings.

choices.text: The step between receiving the catalog tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Re-read the pipeline config again, since that's the earliest step.
Nothing — a wrong report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and catalog data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.

Base64-encode the password before committing it.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk; C doesn't remove the credential either.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected warehouse tools grant broader access (e.g., full `DROP TABLE` rights) than any actual analytics workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add a confirmation prompt before any destructive statement.
Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. B and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

choices.text: Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

The one-off lineage report as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused SLA-status capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, B, and C force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 8.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The agent's harness needs to know when to stop executing tools and hand a finished review back to the paralegal who queued it. Question: What signal should the harness key off? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether `flag_risk` has been called at least once in the conversation.
A hard limit of five tool calls per contract, regardless of context.
Whether the most recent tool call succeeded without an error.
The `stop_reason` field on the response: continue the loop while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Whether a specific tool was called (A), a fixed call cap (B), and error status (C) are all unreliable or secondary signals compared to the authoritative field.

questions.prompt: After `search_clause_library` returns matching precedent clauses, the harness needs the agent to keep reasoning about the contract with that information available. Question: What must the harness do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the corresponding `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.
Write the clause matches to a shared database and let the agent query it separately if needed.
Paste the clause matches into the system prompt so they persist for future contracts too.
Summarize the matches in a new user-authored message unrelated to the tool call.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent. Writing to a separate database (B) hides the result from the model; the system prompt (C) is the wrong place for turn-level data; a plain user message (D) breaks the expected tool-result linkage.

questions.prompt: Firm policy requires a licensed partner to approve any recommendation to reject a vendor contract outright. The system prompt states this rule clearly, but an audit finds the agent occasionally recommended outright rejection without triggering `request_partner_review`. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the rule near the end of the system prompt as well as the beginning.
Add several few-shot examples of the agent correctly escalating rejection recommendations.
Lower the temperature so the agent follows written policy more consistently.
Implement a hook that intercepts any final review output recommending rejection and blocks delivery unless `request_partner_review` was called first.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks delivery outright. Repeating the rule (A), few-shot examples (B), and lowering temperature (C) all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing.

State in the system prompt that clause-library lookup must always happen first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so some tool call is guaranteed.
Add several few-shot transcripts showing the clause lookup running first.

questions.explanation: Forcing tool choice on a specific tool guarantees it runs first; later turns proceed normally. A system-prompt statement (B) and `tool_choice: "any"` (C) don't guarantee which tool runs; few-shot examples (D) remain probabilistic.

The agent responds inconsistently to each case. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

Add a system-prompt note asking the agent to infer the failure type from context.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each distinct failure. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (B) is worse than the tool reporting it; a longer timeout (D) reduces frequency without fixing missing information.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Incident-Response Ops Agent for a Cloud Hosting Provider (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: NimbusHost operates virtual machines and managed containers for thousands of customers. The platform team is building "Aegis," an internal incident-response agent built on the Claude Agent SDK, with custom tools including `check_node_status`, `restart_container`, `scale_replica_pool`, `open_customer_incident`, and `escalate_to_oncall`. Several of these tools are destructive or customer-visible, so how tool access is granted and enforced matters as much as Aegis's reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants Aegis's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until Claude has no further tool calls to make. What should the loop's continue/stop decision key off?

choices.text: The `stop_reason` value returned with each response: continue while it equals `tool_use`, stop once it becomes `end_turn`.
A hard limit of 5 tool calls per session, regardless of content.
Scanning the assistant's text for phrases like "issue resolved."
Whether the most recent tool call took longer than 2 seconds to return.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (C) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; call duration (D) doesn't indicate completion.

questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent's tool-use loop must decide when to stop executing tools and hand control back to the human ops queue. What should drive that decision?

choices.text: Whether the last tool result contains the word "complete."
A hard limit of five tool calls per order.
Whether the model's response text is longer than 200 tokens.
The `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools while it equals `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; response length (C) says nothing about completion.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP tool for crash data, and writes a triage report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid crash data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
Just the final error message, since the human can re-investigate from there.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; B skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. B and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

(Select ONE response.)

Build an MCP server exposing crash-reporting operations as tools, shared across the org and maintained centrally by the platform team.
Hard-code crash-reporting logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the crash-reporting API manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.

MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the mobile repository, currently has an app-store-metadata API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. B is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; C and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full crash-log deletion rights) than any actual mobile engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: An engineer builds a tool-execution loop for the research agent that must keep calling tools and returning results until Claude has nothing more to do on its own. What should the loop check to decide when to stop?

choices.text: Continue while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.
Stop as soon as `find_contacts` has been called once.
Stop after a fixed 5-second timer regardless of tool calls.
Stop when the response text contains the word "brief."

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (D) are unreliable; a single-call stop (B) or fixed timer (C) don't reflect what Claude actually needs.

questions.prompt: After `pull_funding_data` runs, what must the integration code do so Claude can correctly reason about the result on the next turn?

choices.text: Insert the raw funding data directly into a new system prompt for the remainder of the session.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.
Store the funding data in the CRM database only; the model doesn't need to see it directly.
Start a new session and paste a summary of the funding data as the first user message.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. C keeps the result from the model entirely. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

Remove or scope out the tools unrelated to the agent's core sales-research role.

Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to infer the failure type from context.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Fernhollow Marketplace runs a catalog enrichment pipeline that generates product descriptions, assigns categories, and extracts attributes (size, material, color) from seller-submitted text and images. It handles both interactive single-listing requests and nightly batch jobs covering hundreds of thousands of listings.
questions.prompt: The nightly job processes 200,000 listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model to reduce cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed results back to the model within a single request — required for this iterative loop.
The 24-hour window makes any retry logic impossible.
The Batch API's context window is too small for listing text.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

Increasing `max_tokens` so the full response arrives faster.
Polling the Batch API status endpoint every second.
Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. A is the wrong API for this use case; B and C don't address perceived latency.

questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 5,000-token attribute taxonomy and style guide, followed by the listing-specific text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests?

choices.text: Move the taxonomy into a few-shot example block instead.
Place the stable taxonomy and style guide first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying listing text last.
Truncate the taxonomy to save tokens.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of extraction quality.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The schema requires a `material` field on every listing. Many listings genuinely don't specify material, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding materials rather than reporting unknown. Question: What schema change fixes this?

choices.text: Remove the field from the schema entirely.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent values.
