questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: Most report sections are short, templated commentary (e.g., a routine "expense summary") generated at high volume with simple structure. Latency and cost matter far more than handling rare, highly complex sections well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every section.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity sections, reserving a higher tier only for sections flagged as complex.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the firm's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity sections fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of report sections require tracing a multi-entity intercompany reconciliation, where the fast default model produces shallow, incomplete commentary. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every section.
Switch every section to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Route only the flagged complex sections to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Increase max_tokens for all sections.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex sections to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, report tone and numeric-citation style shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B accepts avoidable risk; A and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: Reports need a consistent structure (executive summary, variance analysis, notable transactions, outlook) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.
Lower the temperature to zero.
Ask the model to restate the structure before writing the report.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; B and C don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: A client's ledger export is very long (thousands of transaction rows). The team wants a maximally detailed narrative and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.
Output length has no effect on latency.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long input leaves less room for a long output, and vice versa.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, B, and C misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: The reporting prompt currently places the specific transaction data before the general reporting instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or placed first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; transaction-specific content should come after as the varying part.
Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. B, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the reporting service costs per client report, but the team currently estimates cost only from average ledger-export length. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per report, used as a cost proxy.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per report, rather than an estimate from average length.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on transaction-row count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per report gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (A, C, D) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the generated variance-analysis paragraph must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even though the reports look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and C misdiagnose the cause; B doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: Ledger exports include full raw metadata for every transaction (internal batch codes, system timestamps, routing IDs) that bloats the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase max_tokens to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before generating the report.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and B work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. Reports must follow a consistent structure and cite figures precisely, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit quality and cost targets.
questions.prompt: For clients with very long transaction histories, the team notices generated reports consistently miss mid-period transactions while capturing the opening and closing period well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Put a brief overview or key-figures summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed transactions under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole period."
Alphabetize the transactions before summarizing.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-figures summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; C and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. questions.prompt: A generated report confidently states a reconciled balance that, on manual review, never actually appears anywhere in the source ledger. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches a client? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default.
Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., stated balances) against the source ledger rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Shorten the report so there's less room for errors.

choices.text: Repeat the JSON instruction more emphatically.
Increase max_tokens so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`.

questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates quarterly financial reports — narrative commentary plus supporting tables — for mid-market clients from raw general-ledger exports and transaction histories. questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a client's prior-quarter reports for context before drafting the current one, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load the entire prior-quarter report history directly into the main prompt every time.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main drafting step.

questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer using the Claude Agent SDK. It handles order-fulfillment exceptions — backorders, address problems, damaged-item claims, and refund requests — using custom tools (`check_inventory`, `create_shipping_label`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`). Refunds and label creation carry real financial and operational cost, so tool access and enforcement matter as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent calls `create_shipping_label` and `issue_refund` tools within a single turn. What should the orchestration code key off to know whether to keep executing tool calls and feeding results back, versus finishing the turn?

choices.text: Whether the agent's text includes phrases like "order resolved."
A hard limit of 5 tool calls per order.
Whether the last tool call succeeded without errors.
The `stop_reason` value returned with the response: keep looping while it is `"tool_use"`, stop when it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; tool errors (C) don't indicate loop completion.

Store the inventory count in a database and let the agent infer it was checked.
Insert the result into the system prompt for the remainder of the session.
End the turn and start a new conversation summarizing the inventory count.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: The nightly job reprocesses 25,000 stored documents across all tenants with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model to reduce cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. C doesn't reduce per-token cost; B and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that triages hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day — classifying category, urgency, and suggested team — before a human ever sees them. questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage classification task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every ticket.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity tasks, reserving a higher tier only for tickets flagged as complex.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every ticket.
Switch every ticket to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all tickets.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on ticket character count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the triage category output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample ticket, and the eval fails intermittently even though the categorizations look correct on manual review. What is the most likely issue with the eval design?

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.prompt: Ticket threads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every message, including internal routing headers) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before triaging.
Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; A adds cost without fixing anything.

questions.prompt: For very long ticket threads, the team notices triage decisions consistently miss details from the middle of the conversation while capturing the opening and closing messages well. What is the most effective mitigation?

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole conversation."
Alphabetize the messages before triaging.

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A triage rationale confidently states that a customer already received a refund, but on manual review, no refund was ever issued in the ticket thread. What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches routing?

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., "refund issued") against the source thread rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Shorten the rationale so there's less room for errors.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source thread catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. What is the more reliable approach?

choices.text: Repeat the JSON instruction more emphatically.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

choices.text: Load the entire ticket history directly into the main prompt every time.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main triage step.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.

For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a 20-engineer mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code locally and in CI for PR review, release-note generation, and native-dependency auditing. The team also relies on MCP servers for its issue tracker, build-status system, and internal design docs. You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the mobile team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established Kotlin/Swift style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. B, C, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a 20-engineer mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code locally and in CI for PR review, release-note generation, and native-dependency auditing. questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to generate release notes from merged PRs and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.prompt: A downstream release dashboard parses Claude Code's release-notes output with regex to categorize entries, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Post the entire raw output as a single changelog entry instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the release-notes structure for machine-parseable output.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, B, and C are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-native-libs` custom command prints thousands of lines of native-dependency graph data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so developers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. B restricts capability, not output destination; A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-screen` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; B mitigates damage rather than preventing it; C is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how push-notification handling flows across a large, unfamiliar codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read every file in the codebase in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; B frees trivial space while losing standards; C describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP tool for build status, and writes a QA report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and D re-check or skip already-verified steps; B skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A and B guess without diagnosis; C doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.prompt: The internal issue-tracking system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole mobile organization, not just one squad, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming application. What is the best approach?

Build an MCP server exposing issue-tracking operations as tools, shared across the org.
Have each team paste issue-tracker API credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code issue-tracking logic into each squad's custom skill separately.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

A Claude Code Skill.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.

questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the build-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. What should drive the decision?

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has an issue-tracker API token hardcoded directly in the file. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${ISSUE_TRACKER_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full issue-deletion rights) than any actual mobile-team workflow requires. What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. B and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, squad-specific release-checklist workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused build-status-checking capability needed by every agent across the mobile org. How should each be built?

choices.text: Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.

The one-off release-checklist workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that squad; the widely-reused build-status capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a mid-market B2B SaaS company, is building an internal Claude Agent SDK research agent that preps account executives before sales calls. The main agent orchestrates subagents — a company-researcher, a contacts-finder, and a competitive-analyst — and has tools including `search_web`, `get_crm_record`, `enrich_contact`, and `log_research_note`.
questions.prompt: The main research agent calls `search_web` multiple times in sequence, each time waiting for results before deciding what to do next. What should determine when the tool-use loop stops iterating?

choices.text: When `log_research_note` has been called at least once.
A fixed cap of exactly 3 `search_web` calls per prospect.
When the conversation exceeds 4,000 tokens.
The API response's `stop_reason`: keep executing tool calls while it is `"tool_use"`, stop when it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; token count (C) doesn't indicate loop completion.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a mid-market B2B SaaS company, is building an internal Claude Agent SDK research agent that preps account executives before sales calls. questions.prompt: After the `enrich_contact` tool executes and your code runs it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the contact?

choices.text: Summarize the enrichment result into the system prompt for future turns.
Save the enrichment result to the CRM only, without informing the agent.
Start a new conversation turn that references the enrichment output by ID.
Append a `tool_result` block tied to the original `tool_use` ID and resend the full conversation to the model.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data; B keeps the result from the model entirely; C discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Meridian's compliance team requires that `log_research_note` never record data sourced from a prospect's personal social media profile, regardless of what the agent reasons about mid-task. The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show it happened anyway. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Restate the rule more forcefully at the very top of the prompt.
Add few-shot examples of the agent correctly declining to log personal social data.
Reduce temperature so instructions are followed more literally.
Add a hook that inspects `log_research_note` calls and blocks any whose content is tagged as sourced from personal social media.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. A, B, and C all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernbridge Marketplace lets sellers upload raw product listings — title, bullet points, sometimes a photo — in bulk. Claude enriches each listing into structured attributes (category, material, dimensions, safety flags) used for search and filtering. The pipeline handles both an interactive single-listing flow (a seller uploads one item and waits) and a nightly batch flow (hundreds of thousands of listings).
questions.prompt: The nightly batch job enriches 200,000 listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step needs a tool call mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model to reduce cost.
The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and C risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't support system prompts.
The 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic impossible.
The Batch API's context window is too small for long listings.
The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed results back to the model within a single request — required for this iterative loop.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and C misidentify the actual limitation.

Place the stable schema and taxonomy reference first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying listing text last.

Start a fresh session (or `/compact`) at natural task boundaries, such as between different sellers' batches, rather than accumulating unrelated context in one long session.
Ask the model to "ignore earlier listings" at the start of each new batch.
Increase the context window so more history fits without confusion.

questions.explanation: Resetting at natural task boundaries prevents unrelated context from bleeding into new work. C is unreliable prompt-level mitigation; A is an unrelated lever; D doesn't address cross-contamination.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Codeforge runs an internal code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across a large monorepo, summarizing changes, flagging risks, and suggesting fixes. It runs on every PR, so cost and latency matter, but a small fraction of PRs are complex refactors that need deeper reasoning.
questions.prompt: Most PRs are small and reviewable with straightforward checks; latency and cost per PR matter far more than handling rare, highly complex refactors well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity review, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every PR.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the hardest architectural reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. B and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant

questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs are complex multi-file refactors where the fast default model produces shallow, generic review comments. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every PR.
Route only the flagged complex PRs to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every PR to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all PRs.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The service floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review tone and the kinds of issues flagged shifted noticeably with no code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.prompt: Reviews need a consistent structure (summary, risk level, specific issues, suggested fix), but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.
Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.
Lower the temperature to zero.
Ask the model to restate the structure before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. B repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.prompt: A PR diff is very large (2,000+ changed lines). The team wants a maximally detailed review and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long diff leaves less room for a long review, and vice versa.
Output length has no effect on latency.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long diff directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The review prompt currently places the specific diff text before the general review instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or placed first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; diff-specific content should come after as the varying part.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the review assistant costs per PR, but the team currently estimates cost only from average diff size. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per PR, rather than an estimate from average size.
Wall-clock latency per PR, used as a cost proxy.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on diff line count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average size or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the review output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample PR, and the eval fails intermittently even though the reviews look correct on manual read. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant

questions.prompt: PR diffs include full raw CI-log dumps attached to every review request, most of it irrelevant noise, bloating the prompt and slowing the pipeline. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prune the CI output to the relevant fields (failures, relevant lines) before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the CI logs with a second Claude call before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. C and D work around the symptom without reducing waste; B adds cost without addressing the root problem.

questions.prompt: For very long PR diffs, reviewers notice the assistant consistently misses issues in the middle of the diff while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the diff and organize file-by-file changes under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole diff."
Alphabetize the files before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear file headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; C and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A review confidently states that a particular function is now covered by a new test, but on manual check, no such test exists in the diff. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the PR? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., "test coverage" statements) against the actual diff rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Shorten the review so there's less room for errors.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the actual diff catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; C and D don't address correctness.

choices.text: Repeat the JSON instruction more emphatically.
Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a file's past PR history for context before reviewing the current change, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main review step.
Load the entire file history directly into the main prompt every time.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. B and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common PR type (dependency version bumps), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. Question: What consideration should drive the choice? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Multi-shot is always strictly better regardless of task simplicity.
For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.
Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. A, B, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. The platform team is responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new data engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, C, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review data-pipeline pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's pipeline-review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-schema` custom command prints thousands of lines of table and column metadata, and engineers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
`argument-hint`, so engineers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario_context: Northlake's data-engineering team supports about 30 engineers using Claude Code alongside a set of internal MCP servers: a warehouse-query server, a pipeline-status server, and a data-catalog server. questions.prompt: An internal `/new-pipeline` skill is meant only to scaffold new pipeline files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require engineers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar ETL codebase's data-lineage tracking works before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.

Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; B frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls an internal MCP warehouse-query tool, and writes a status report produces a wrong final report. choices.text: The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A, B, and D guess or fail to investigate the cause.

questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${WAREHOUSE_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Locke LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, is deploying a contract-review agent to help attorneys review vendor contracts, NDAs, and lease agreements. The agent has tools including `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `redline_suggest`, and `request_attorney_review`. Because incorrect redlines or missed risk flags carry real legal and financial consequences, tool design and escalation policy matter as much as review quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants the contract-review agent's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until Claude has no more tool calls to make. What should the loop key off?

The `stop_reason` field on each response: continue looping while it is `"tool_use"`, stop when it is `"end_turn"`.
A hard cap of five tool calls per contract.
Whether `flag_risk` returned any flags.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (C) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; whether flags were found (D) doesn't indicate loop completion.

questions.scenario_context: Helios Connect, a SaaS company, is integrating Claude into its live customer-support chat widget, where Claude drafts responses to customers in real time alongside human agents, occasionally calling tools (`search_kb`, `create_ticket`, `check_order_status`).

choices.text: Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.
The Batch API, since it's designed for real-time feedback.
Increasing max_tokens so the full response arrives faster.
Polling a status endpoint every second.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time chat UIs. B is the wrong API for this use case; C and D don't address perceived latency.

choices.text: The Batch API, because it's cheaper per token.
The Batch API, because it supports mid-request tool calls.
The synchronous Messages API with streaming, since the customer is waiting live and the flow needs a tool call answered within the same request.
The synchronous Messages API without streaming, since streaming and tool use are mutually exclusive.

questions.explanation: A customer waiting live for a reply that requires a mid-request tool call needs the synchronous Messages API (with streaming for responsiveness); the Batch API cannot answer a tool call within a single request the way this flow needs. A and B misdescribe the Batch API; D is a false claim — streaming and tool use are not mutually exclusive.

Switch to the smallest available model regardless of quality.
Place the stable policy/tone instructions first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying conversation history after it.
Truncate the policy text to save tokens.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

Convert thinking output into a separate tool call.
Discard thinking content only when tools are involved.
Handle the thinking content block as distinct from the final answer text, typically preserving it appropriately across the multi-turn tool-use conversation.

Only output tokens, since input is effectively free.
Input tokens, output tokens, and cache read/write tokens, since each is priced differently.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Optimizing a Multilingual Content-Moderation Service
questions.scenario_context: GlobalGuard operates a content-moderation service that classifies user-generated posts across 40 languages for policy violations, processing millions of posts per day. Cost, latency, and consistency across languages all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most posts are short and moderation is a simple binary classification (violates / doesn't violate) at extremely high volume. Latency and cost per post matter far more than handling rare, ambiguous edge cases well. Which approach best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every post.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity classification, reserving a higher tier only for posts flagged as ambiguous.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity classification fits a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged ambiguous cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend or ignore fit by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Optimizing a Multilingual Content-Moderation Service
questions.scenario_context: GlobalGuard operates a content-moderation service that classifies user-generated posts across 40 languages for policy violations, processing millions of posts per day. Cost, latency, and consistency across languages all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of posts require nuanced judgment (satire versus genuine hate speech, or context-dependent slang) where the fast default model produces inconsistent classifications. What is the most targeted fix?

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every post.
Route only the flagged ambiguous posts to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every post to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase max_tokens for all posts.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged ambiguous cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The service floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, classification thresholds shifted noticeably for borderline posts, with no code change on the team's side. What should the team do differently?

choices.text: Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B accepts avoidable risk; C and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.prompt: Moderation output needs a consistent label set (`hate_speech`, `harassment`, `spam`, `none`), but detailed prose instructions describing the categories haven't produced consistent output across languages. What technique is most likely to help?

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the categories.
Lower the temperature to zero.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples in multiple languages demonstrating the exact desired labeling.
Ask the model to restate the categories before classifying.

questions.explanation: Concrete, multilingual few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent labeling when prose alone hasn't worked across languages. A repeats a failed approach; B and D don't reliably fix structural/labeling consistency.

questions.prompt: The moderation prompt currently places the specific post text before the general policy instructions and desired label format in every request. Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability?

choices.text: Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Stable, role-defining policy instructions belong first (system prompt or first block) so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; post-specific content should come after as the varying part.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the moderation service costs per post, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. What should be instrumented instead?

choices.text: Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per post, rather than an estimate from average length.
Wall-clock latency per post, used as a cost proxy.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on post character count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per post gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (B, C, D) don't.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the moderation label must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample post, and the eval fails intermittently even though the labels look correct on manual review. What is the most likely issue with the eval design?

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario_context: GlobalGuard operates a content-moderation service that classifies user-generated posts across 40 languages for policy violations, processing millions of posts per day. questions.prompt: Posts arrive with full raw platform metadata dumps (every field of the post object) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase max_tokens to accommodate the extra data.
Prune the metadata to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before classifying.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.prompt: For very long comment threads, the team notices moderation misses violations in the middle of the thread while catching issues in the opening and closing comments well. What is the most effective mitigation?

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole thread."
Alphabetize the comments before classifying.

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A moderation report confidently states a post "contains a direct threat of violence," but on manual review the post was actually a quote from a news article being discussed critically. What practice would most help catch this class of error before action is taken?

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default.
Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Shorten the report so there's less room for errors.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims against the source post rather than accepting fluency as correctness.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source post catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and C don't address correctness.

Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.

Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main moderation step.

questions.prompt: For the simplest, most common moderation case (obvious spam links), the team is deciding between a zero-shot prompt and a multi-shot prompt with several examples. What consideration should drive the choice?

choices.text: Multi-shot is always strictly better regardless of task simplicity.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.
For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and B are absolute claims that don't hold generally; C is false.

Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.
