questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new QA engineer clones the team's test-automation repo, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established test-naming and assertion conventions, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new engineer cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to triage failing test runs and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The test runs are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A downstream dashboard parses Claude Code's test-triage output with regex to auto-file defect tickets, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the triage-findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-parsing requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `/scan-flaky-tests` custom command prints thousands of lines of historical test-run data, and testers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so testers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C restricts capability, not output destination; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/generate-test-fixtures` skill is meant only to create new fixture files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated config files. What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require testers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; B mitigates damage rather than preventing it; C is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A QA engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar test-automation framework's fixture system works before writing new tests, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read every file in the framework in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; C doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the new tests in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a test-config file, calls an internal MCP tool to fetch environment status, and writes a defect-triage report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and B re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A test-environment provisioning tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A and B guess without diagnosis; C doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The internal defect-tracking system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole QA org, not just one team, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming application. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Build an MCP server exposing defect-tracking operations as tools, shared across the org.
Have each team paste defect-tracker API credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code defect-tracking logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the defect-tracker API manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. B, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An MCP server for the test-case management system exposes both a `search_test_cases` tool and a way for agents to see what test suites exist without an exploratory search call. What is the second capability an example of?

choices.text: An MCP tool, functionally identical to `search_test_cases`.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
A Claude Code Skill.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. A, C, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether an internal MCP server for test-environment provisioning should run as a local stdio process per QA engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. What should drive the decision?

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and C are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a defect-tracker API token hardcoded directly in the file. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${DEFECT_TRACKER_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full test-suite deletion rights) than any actual QA workflow requires. What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and D are detective/compensating controls; B accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support a 30-person QA team's use of Claude Code, custom skills, slash commands, and internal MCP servers (test-case management, defect tracking, test-environment provisioning). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.

choices.text: The one-off report-formatting workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused environment-health-check capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Incident-Response Ops Agent for a Cloud Hosting Provider
questions.scenario_context: Kestrel Cloud runs virtual-machine and container hosting for mid-market customers. Its SRE team is building "Warden," an on-call assistant built on the Claude Agent SDK with custom tools (`check_node_health`, `restart_container`, `rotate_api_key`, `notify_customer`, `page_sre`). Warden triages incidents overnight before a human ever looks at them, so tool-execution correctness and guardrails matter as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: Warden's harness needs to know when to keep feeding tool results back to the model versus when the model is finished responding for the turn. Question: What should the harness check? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether the assistant's text includes phrases like "incident resolved."
A hardcoded limit of eight tool calls per session.
Whether `notify_customer` has been called yet.
The `stop_reason` on the response: keep looping while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text keywords (A) are unreliable, a call-count cap (B) is only a backstop, and waiting on a specific tool (C) doesn't reflect turn completion generally.

questions.prompt: After Warden calls `rotate_api_key` and the harness executes it, what is required for Warden to reason correctly about the outcome on its next turn?

choices.text: Log the rotation to the audit database and let the next prompt reference it by ticket number.
Summarize the rotation result in a fresh system prompt for a new session.
Append the rotated key's confirmation to the end of the system prompt so it persists.
Add a `tool_result` block keyed to the original `tool_use` ID into the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be attached as a `tool_result` block referencing the original `tool_use` ID and the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate it. Logging elsewhere (A) keeps the result out of the model's reasoning; C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data; D-as-new-session (labeled B here) discards useful state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Kestrel's policy requires a human approve any `restart_container` call targeting a customer's primary database container. Add several few-shot transcripts showing Warden escalating instead of restarting.
Lower temperature so Warden follows written policy more literally.
Add a hook that intercepts `restart_container` calls and blocks any targeting a database container unless a human-approval flag is already set.

questions.explanation: A safety-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright; prompt placement (A), few-shot examples (B), and temperature (C) all remain probabilistic compliance, which is exactly what's failing.

questions.prompt: The SRE team wants Warden to always call `check_node_health` first on every incident, with zero exceptions, before considering any other tool. Question: What is the most reliable way to enforce this? (Select ONE response.)

Set `tool_choice` to force `check_node_health` specifically on the first request, then revert to normal tool choice afterward.
Provide five few-shot examples that all open with `check_node_health`.

questions.explanation: Forcing tool choice to a specific tool on the first turn guarantees it runs first; normal choice resumes afterward. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees a call but not which one; A and D remain probabilistic.

Add a "primary tools" note to the system prompt listing which ones matter most.
Increase `max_tokens` so Warden has more room to think through tool choice.
Rename the unrelated tools with less appealing descriptions so Warden avoids them.

Warden's downstream behavior is inconsistent across these cases. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Return structured error data: a category (not-found, timeout, permission), a retryable flag, and a short human-readable description.
Have Warden guess the cause from surrounding conversation context.
Wrap every call in an automatic three-retry policy regardless of cause.
Extend the health-check agent's timeout so timeouts occur less often.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each distinct failure mode. Model-driven selection is always cheaper because it uses fewer tokens.
A fixed script would require rewriting all of Warden's tool schemas.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Batch Invoice-Extraction Pipeline for a Logistics Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Logistics runs a nightly pipeline that extracts structured line-item data from carrier invoices — tens of thousands per night — plus a smaller interactive flow where a billing clerk uploads a single disputed invoice and waits for results. Some invoices are scanned images with degraded OCR, and the pipeline is being expanded to run across multiple regional cloud vendors.
questions.prompt: The nightly job processes 60,000 carrier invoices with no user waiting on any individual result, and no step needs Claude to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API, run across as many parallel threads as the rate limit allows.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` set to the minimum possible value.
The synchronous Messages API paired with the smallest available model.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the real cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Batch Invoice-Extraction Pipeline for a Logistics Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Logistics runs a nightly pipeline that extracts structured line-item data from carrier invoices — tens of thousands per night — plus a smaller interactive flow where a billing clerk uploads a single disputed invoice and waits for results. questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract, validate line totals, retry any failed fields" loop to the nightly pipeline and proposes running that entire loop inside the Batch API to keep the cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API doesn't accept system prompts.
Batch requests are capped at a context window too small for multi-page invoices.
The Batch API can't execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — which this iterative loop requires.
The 24-hour batch window makes any retry logic technically impossible.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.prompt: The interactive single-invoice flow shows the billing clerk a live, incrementally-updating view of the extraction as it happens. Question: What technique best supports this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Polling the Batch API's status endpoint every second.
Streaming, so the UI can render partial output as it arrives and reduce perceived latency.
Raising `max_tokens` so the full response completes sooner.
The Batch API, since it's optimized for real-time feedback.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, which is what reduces perceived latency for a live progress view. D is the wrong API for this use case; A and C don't address perceived latency.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Freight Logistics runs a nightly pipeline that extracts structured line-item data from carrier invoices — tens of thousands per night — plus a smaller interactive flow where a billing clerk uploads a single disputed invoice and waits for results. Some invoices are scanned images with degraded OCR, and the pipeline is being expanded to run across multiple regional cloud vendors.
questions.prompt: Every extraction request sends the same 5,500-token field-schema and carrier-code reference, followed by invoice-specific text that varies per request. Question: What single change most directly reduces both latency and cost across the whole pipeline? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the schema reference into a few-shot example instead of prose.
Place the stable schema/instructions first, enable prompt caching on that prefix, and put the varying invoice text last.
Truncate the carrier-code reference to the most common carriers only.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of extraction quality impact.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable, so placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits and reduces both latency and cost. A, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: Two extraction passes on the same invoice disagree on a weight field — one reads 2,140 lb, the other 2,410 lb — and there is no way to resolve the discrepancy from the surrounding text. Question: What should the pipeline do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Always trust whichever pass ran first.
Average the two readings.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source, rather than silently picking one.
Discard the invoice entirely as unreliable.

questions.explanation: Conflicting reads with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The pipeline's free-text JSON extraction output fails to parse cleanly on roughly 4% of runs, crashing the downstream loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask for YAML instead, since it tolerates minor formatting drift better.
Add a JSON-repair library step before parsing.
Retry with "return valid JSON only" appended to the prompt whenever a parse fails.
Define a tool whose input schema matches the extraction structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating this parsing-failure class outright. A and B are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; C swaps one fragile text format for another.

questions.prompt: After switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, output always parses successfully, but some line-item amounts still don't sum to the invoice's stated total. Question: What should you conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Strict schemas guarantee syntactic validity, not semantic correctness — add a separate validation step checking totals against summed line items.
`max_tokens` must be too low, truncating output mid-generation.
The schema needs stricter numeric types.
Abandon tool use and return to free-text extraction with manual review.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step checking totals against summed line items is needed on top. B, C, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

Switch to a larger model, since bigger models always parse noisy OCR better.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ashcroft & Vale, a mid-size accounting firm, runs a service that turns structured quarterly ledger data into narrative sections of client-facing financial reports — hundreds of reports per week during close season. The team is tuning model selection, prompt structure, and context handling to keep cost, latency, and factual reliability under control.
questions.prompt: Most report sections are short, formulaic narrative (e.g., "revenue summary") generated at high volume, where speed and cost per section matter far more than rare, deeply complex cases. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whichever tier is cheapest per token, independent of task fit.
The same tier used for the firm's hardest audit-reasoning work, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity generation, reserving a higher tier only for sections flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every section.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity generation fits a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex sections — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; B ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Prompt and Context Engineering for a Financial-Reporting Generator
questions.scenario_context: Ashcroft & Vale, a mid-size accounting firm, runs a service that turns structured quarterly ledger data into narrative sections of client-facing financial reports — hundreds of reports per week during close season. questions.prompt: A small fraction of report sections require multi-step reasoning (reconciling a multi-entity intercompany transfer) where the fast default model produces shallow, occasionally wrong narrative. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` across the board for every section.
Switch every report section to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Route only the flagged complex sections to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for all sections.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex sections to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The service currently always calls "whatever model is latest." After a routine model update, report tone and section structure shifted noticeably with no code change on Ashcroft & Vale's side. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Disable prompt caching to prevent drift.
Nothing — behavioral drift across model releases is expected and needs no process.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Permanently roll back to the oldest available model version.

questions.explanation: Pinning a version and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B accepts avoidable risk; A and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.prompt: Report sections need a consistent structure (headline figure, drivers, comparison to prior period, outlook), but detailed prose instructions describing that structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask the model to restate the structure before writing the section.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.
Lower temperature to zero.
Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. D repeats a failed approach; A and C don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.prompt: A ledger detail input is unusually long (a full year of transaction-level entries), and the team wants a maximally detailed narrative output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long input leaves less room for a long output, and vice versa.
Output length has no bearing on latency.
Input and output tokens are budgeted entirely independently of one another.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, C, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.prompt: The report-generation prompt currently places the specific client's ledger data before the general narrative-writing instructions and formatting rules in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Placing instructions last always improves how carefully the model attends to them.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong first (or in the system prompt) to form a consistent, cacheable prefix, while the client-specific ledger data — which varies — should come after.
Reordering affects cost only, never consistency.
Order has no measurable effect on either consistency or caching.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) with variable content after improves both clear role separation (consistency) and caching. A, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per report, rather than an estimate from average length.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token volume.
Wall-clock latency per report, used as a cost proxy.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per report gives an accurate cost picture; estimates or unrelated proxies (A, C, D) don't.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval asserting that a report section's output must exactly match a fixed reference string, and the eval fails intermittently even though manual review shows the generated sections are correct. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Temperature should be raised to fix the intermittent failures.
LLM output is inherently non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation and check for required content/structure instead.
The reference string needs to be longer.
The model is broken and producing incorrect narrative.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.prompt: Ledger exports include full raw metadata for every transaction (internal system IDs, timestamps down to the millisecond, batch codes) that bloats the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have a second Claude call summarize the raw metadata before the main narrative call.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Prune the export to relevant financial fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Raise `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra metadata.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and D add cost or complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering; B works around the symptom without reducing waste.

questions.prompt: For unusually long report sections drawing on a full year of ledger history, the generated narrative consistently captures the opening and closing quarters well but misses details from the middle of the year. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the model to "weigh all quarters equally."
Switch to a model with an even larger context window.

Put a brief key-facts overview at the start of the input and organize detailed quarter-by-quarter data under clear section headers, countering the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Sort the ledger entries alphabetically by account name before summarizing.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. B is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; A and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

Raise temperature so the model sounds less confident.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims against the source ledger data rather than accepting fluency as correctness.

Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main drafting step.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.

Multi-shot is always strictly better, regardless of task simplicity.

Rewrite the prompt from scratch every quarter.
Allow only one designated analyst to ever read the prompt.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: A newly hired engineer clones a Corvid repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level configuration that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new engineer cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Corvid Systems has grown from 12 to 85 engineers in a year. Its platform team now owns Claude Code standards across the org, several internal MCP servers (ticketing, deployment status, internal wiki), and a CI pipeline that runs Claude Code headlessly for automated PR review.
questions.prompt: Corvid's nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.
The pull requests being reviewed are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, B, and C are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
Nothing — a wrong report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal agent for a mid-size e-commerce retailer's warehouse operations team using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reroute_shipment`, `issue_refund`, `notify_customer`) and helps ops staff resolve stuck orders and delayed shipments. Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants the agent's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until the model has no more tool calls to make. What should the loop key off?

choices.text: Whether the response text contains a word like "resolved."
A fixed cap of 5 tool calls per case, regardless of content.
Whether the most recent tool call returned an error.
The `stop_reason` field: continue while it is `"tool_use"`, terminate at `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; tool errors (C) don't indicate loop completion.

Reroutes and refunds carry real logistics and financial cost, so tool governance matters as much as reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: After the agent calls `reroute_shipment` and your code executes it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the case?

choices.text: Store the reroute confirmation in an internal log only.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID to the conversation, then send the full conversation back to the model.
Summarize the result into the system prompt so it persists for the rest of the conversation.
Start a new session summarizing the reroute and continue there.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. A keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity tasks, reserving a higher tier only for tickets flagged as complex.
The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every ticket.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. B and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every ticket.
Switch every ticket to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase max_tokens for all tickets.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run a service that classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of inbound support tickets per day into the correct queue and priority level. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The triage prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this?

Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.
Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. B, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to generate release notes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The release notes are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's crash-triage output with regex to file tickets automatically, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-output requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-crashlogs` custom command prints thousands of lines of raw crash-stack data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so developers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C restricts capability, not output destination; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-screen` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how push-notification handling flows across a large, unfamiliar mobile codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read every file in the codebase in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; B frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP crash-reporting tool, and writes a triage report, but produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. B and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.prompt: The internal crash-reporting system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole mobile engineering org, not just one squad, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming app. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Have each squad paste crash-reporting API credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code crash-reporting logic into each squad's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the crash-reporting API manually when needed.
Build an MCP server exposing crash-reporting operations as tools, shared across the org.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-app reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, B, and C all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An MCP server for app-store metadata exposes both a `search_listings` tool and a way for agents to see what metadata categories exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of?

choices.text: An MCP tool, functionally identical to `search_listings`.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
A Claude Code Skill.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether an internal build-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision?

choices.text: Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.
stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. B, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a crash-reporting API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${CRASH_API_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; C and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full crash-log deletion rights) than any actual engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support a mobile app team (iOS and Android) that uses Claude Code both locally and in CI for automated PR review, release-note generation, and crash-log triage. The team relies on internal MCP servers for crash reporting, app-store metadata, and build status.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific release-notes workflow used by a single squad, versus a widely-reused build-status-checking capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built?

choices.text: Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.

The one-off release-notes workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that squad; the widely-reused build-status capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, B, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 7.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The orchestrator agent calls `lookup_company`, receives results, and must decide whether to call another tool or finish. What should the surrounding harness key off to know when to stop feeding tool results back into the loop?

choices.text: Whether the response text contains a phrase like "brief complete."
The `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools and returning results while it is `"tool_use"`, stop once it is `"end_turn"`.
A fixed cap of five tool calls per prospect, regardless of outcome.
Whether `lookup_company` returned a non-empty payload.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Text phrases (A) are unreliable, a fixed cap (C) is a backstop rather than the primary signal, and a non-empty payload (D) doesn't indicate the model is done reasoning.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: After the orchestrator calls `search_news` and the harness executes it, what must happen for the agent to correctly continue reasoning about the prospect?

choices.text: Summarize the news result in a side channel and let the agent ask for it only if it asks.
Store the news result in the CRM and let the agent query the CRM tool again to see it.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the original `tool_use` ID to the conversation, then send the full conversation back to the model.
Rewrite the system prompt to include the news result for the rest of the session.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate it. A and B keep the result out of the model's direct reasoning path; D misuses the system prompt for turn-level data.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: Meridian's policy requires that `send_outreach_email` never fire on a prospect account flagged "do not contact" in the CRM. The system prompt states this rule plainly, but an audit finds a handful of emails sent to flagged accounts anyway. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the "do not contact" rule to the very top of the system prompt for emphasis.
Implement a hook that checks the CRM flag before `send_outreach_email` executes and blocks the call if the account is flagged.
Add few-shot examples showing the agent correctly declining to email flagged accounts.
Lower the model's temperature so instructions are followed more literally.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright when the CRM flag is set. A, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The team wants every research session to begin with `lookup_company` — no exceptions — before any other tool is considered, so the brief always starts from verified firmographic data. Question: What is the most reliable implementation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: State in the system prompt that `lookup_company` must always run first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so some tool call is guaranteed.
Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "lookup_company"}` on the first request, then use normal tool choice afterward.
Add several few-shot examples that show `lookup_company` called first.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed with normal tool choice. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees some tool call, but not which one; A and D are probabilistic.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The orchestrator currently has 14 tools, including several rarely-used ones (partner-referral lookup, event-invite tracking, swag-request submission) that have nothing to do with pre-call research. Tool selection has become unreliable and the agent sometimes calls the wrong tool for a simple company lookup. Question: What is the single most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a system prompt note ranking which tools are "primary" versus "secondary."
Increase max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason before choosing a tool.
Ask the agent to double-check its tool choice with a follow-up message before executing.
Remove the unrelated tools from this agent's tool set — or move them to a separate, specialized agent — so the orchestrator only reasons over tools relevant to pre-call research.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core research role (or splitting them into a separate agent) directly reduces the candidate set the orchestrator must reason over. A adds prompt overhead without removing bloat; B and C don't address the underlying tool-selection problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: `get_crm_history` currently returns the string `"lookup failed"` whether the account ID is invalid, the CRM is down, or the AE lacks access permissions. The agent responds inconsistently to each case. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Wrap every call in an automatic retry policy regardless of cause.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to guess the likely cause from context.
Increase the CRM API's timeout so failures occur less often.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each failure type. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (C) is worse than the tool reporting it; D reduces frequency without fixing the missing information.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: When `search_news` finds no recent articles about a small prospect, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for a "temporary issue" and retrying the identical query. What should change?

choices.text: Add a system prompt note explaining that this particular error usually just means no news exists.
Return a successful response with an empty result list, reserving errors for actual access or service failures.
Have the agent call `lookup_company` again first to confirm the company exists.
Add a hook that silently ends the research session when this happens.

questions.explanation: "No news found" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty list. A patches symptoms while the underlying success/error conflation remains; C invents an unnecessary extra step; D hides real signal from the session.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian Cloud, a B2B SaaS analytics vendor, is building an internal sales-research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: A sales-ops engineer proposes replacing the orchestrator's reasoning with a fixed sequence — always `lookup_company`, then `search_news`, then `get_crm_history`, then draft — arguing it makes output more predictable. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection still the better fit here? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prospect research is high-ambiguity — the right tools, and whether to skip or repeat one, depend on what earlier results reveal, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.
Model-driven selection is always cheaper because it uses fewer reasoning tokens.
Fixed sequences cannot invoke custom tools, only tools built into the platform.
The Claude Agent SDK technically cannot execute a hardcoded tool sequence.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity research where the right tools and order depend on intermediate findings is the core case for model-driven selection. B, C, and D are unsupported claims about the technology.

A narrowly-scoped subagent can be given only the outreach tool and explicit qualification criteria, reducing the chance an email fires while the main agent is reasoning about unrelated research tools.
The main agent's context window is too small to hold the outreach tool's schema.
Any tool with a real-world side effect legally requires a dedicated subagent.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the outreach tool and explicit criteria minimizes accidental sends while the main agent reasons about unrelated tools. A, C, and D are unsupported or overgeneralized technical claims.

The agent has tools (`lookup_company`, `search_news`, `get_crm_history`, `send_outreach_email`, `draft_brief`) and delegates parts of its work to narrowly-scoped subagents so account executives get a concise pre-call brief instead of a wall of raw research.
questions.prompt: The agent finishes a research session and hands the brief to the AE, but the AE has no visibility into what was actually checked — the trace shows a dozen tool calls with no accessible summary of what was tried or found. Question: What should the handoff to the AE include? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Just the final brief text, since the AE doesn't need to know how it was produced.
A structured summary of what was checked, what was found, and any gaps or caveats, alongside the brief.
The full raw transcript of every tool call and result.
A confidence score with no supporting detail.

questions.explanation: A structured summary of what was checked, found, and any gaps lets the AE act with confidence. A omits how the brief was produced; C forces reconstruction from a raw transcript; D conveys a number without substance.

questions.prompt: Meridian is deciding between running the research agent through a hosted, Anthropic-managed execution environment versus self-hosting the agent harness on its own infrastructure. Question: What is the core tradeoff? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Operational control (self-hosted) versus operational burden (managed) — there is no inherent difference in what tools the agent can call.
Self-hosted agents cannot call custom tools like `lookup_company`.
Managed agents are inherently less secure than self-hosted deployments.
Managed agents cannot reach a company's internal CRM under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: The tradeoff is operational control versus operational burden; tool-calling capability doesn't differ between the two deployment models. B, C, and D are unsupported absolute claims.

Whether the task is well-defined and repeatable versus high-ambiguity, where the right steps depend on intermediate findings.

A hook that tracks per-prospect send counts for the day and blocks the tool call once the limit is reached.
