questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The nightly batch enriches 60,000 new listings with no user waiting on the result, and no step requires a mid-request tool call. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API run across as many parallel threads as the account allows, to finish fastest.
The synchronous Messages API with max_tokens set to the minimum needed.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model chosen only to cut cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A and D don't reduce per-token cost the same way; B risks degrading quality without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an "extract attributes, validate against the category schema, retry unresolved fields" loop to the batch pipeline to raise accuracy, and proposes running the entire loop through the Batch API to keep the cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — which this iterative loop requires.
The Batch API's 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic impossible to schedule.
The Batch API doesn't support system prompts, so validation instructions would be dropped.
The Batch API's context window is too small for a full product description.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. B, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The interactive flow shows a seller a live "enriching your listing..." indicator while Claude processes their edit. Question: What technique best supports this experience? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increasing max_tokens so the complete response arrives sooner.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second.
Streaming, so the UI can render partial output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.
Running the request twice and showing whichever finishes first.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for a live "enriching" indicator. A and D don't address perceived latency; B is the wrong API for this use case.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: Every enrichment request sends the same 5,000-token category taxonomy and attribute schema, followed by the specific listing text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Place the stable taxonomy and schema first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying listing text last.
Move the taxonomy into a few-shot example block instead of a schema reference.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of enrichment quality.
Truncate the taxonomy to the most common categories to save tokens.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. B, C, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The attribute schema currently requires a `material` field on every listing. Many listings (e.g., digital gift cards, services) have no physical material, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding materials rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remove the `material` field from the schema entirely.
Lower the temperature to reduce invented values.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent values.
Make `material` nullable so genuine absence can be reported truthfully.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; B and C rely on probabilistic compliance.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: Two enrichment passes on the same listing disagree on size: one reads "Large" and another reads "L," and there's no way to tell from the listing text which normalization the seller intended. Question: What should the pipeline do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source rather than silently picking one.
Always trust whichever pass ran first.
Discard the listing entirely since the data is unreliable.
Average the two representations into a new hybrid value.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. B, C, and D all discard information or guess.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: The enrichment tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream catalog loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Define a `submit_attributes` tool whose input schema matches the attribute structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.
Ask for YAML output instead, since it tolerates minor formatting drift better.
Add a JSON-repair library to patch common syntax issues before parsing.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. B and C are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; D is a retry loop around a still-fragile format.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, enrichment output always parses successfully, but some listings end up with a `category` that doesn't match any `subcategory` in the fixed taxonomy tree. Question: What should you conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The schema needs stricter string types to fix this.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic errors — add a validation step that checks category/subcategory consistency on top of schema compliance.
max_tokens is too low, truncating output before the category is fully written.
Abandon tool use and return to free-text extraction with manual review.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step checking category/subcategory consistency is needed on top. A, C, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Product-Catalog Enrichment Pipeline for an Online Marketplace
questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. The pipeline handles both a large nightly batch of new listings and a smaller interactive flow when a seller edits a listing live on the site.
questions.prompt: A subset of incoming listings have only a low-quality seller photo and almost no text description. The pipeline currently sends only the sparse text to Claude, and enrichment quality is poor for these listings. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Reject listings with insufficient text description from the pipeline entirely.
Send the listing photo itself as an image content block alongside the enrichment instructions, using Claude's native vision input instead of relying solely on sparse text.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models are always better at inferring from little text.
Increase max_tokens so the model can work harder on the sparse description.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses the sparse-text bottleneck entirely. A discards otherwise-processable listings; C and D don't address the actual data-quality gap.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. questions.prompt: The pipeline needs to enrich five sections of a long, multi-variant listing (color options, size chart, care instructions, materials, shipping notes) concurrently to keep total latency reasonable. Question: What must the integration layer support to do this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Streaming, since only streaming supports running more than one request at a time.
A single request with all five sections concatenated, since Claude parallelizes internally.
Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple API calls can be in flight at once without blocking on each other.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to issue more than one request concurrently.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. A, B, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

questions.prompt: Fernhaven plans to run the same enrichment pipeline through both the direct Anthropic API and a third-party cloud vendor's hosted offering for different regional deployments. Question: What should the team expect? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Bedrock-style vendor integrations require an entirely different prompting approach and schema design.
Batch processing is unavailable through any third-party vendor integration.
Enrichment accuracy and latency are guaranteed to be identical to the millisecond across vendors.
The Messages API contract stays conceptually the same across vendors, though auth/plumbing and feature-rollout timing can differ.

questions.explanation: The Messages API contract is conceptually consistent across vendors, though plumbing and rollout timing can differ — this is the realistic expectation, not identical latency or unavailable features.

questions.scenario_context: Fernhaven Marketplace uses Claude to enrich seller-submitted product listings — normalizing titles, inferring categories, and extracting structured attributes (size, material, color) from free-text descriptions and photos. questions.prompt: The team enables extended thinking on a complex multi-step enrichment-and-validation task that uses tool calls across several turns. Question: What must the integration layer do correctly? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Convert thinking output into an additional tool call automatically.
Discard thinking content whenever a tool is also invoked in the same turn.
Handle the thinking content block as distinct from the final answer text, typically preserving it appropriately across the multi-turn tool-use conversation.
Ignore thinking content entirely, since it never affects downstream turns.

questions.explanation: Thinking content is a distinct block type that must be handled (and typically preserved) separately from final answer text across multi-turn tool-use conversations. A, B, and D mishandle or misdescribe this.

questions.prompt: Finance asks for an accurate per-listing cost breakdown for the enrichment pipeline, but the current cost model only estimates based on average description length. Question: What should the improved cost model account for separately? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Input tokens, output tokens, and cache read/write tokens, since each is priced differently.
Only output tokens, since input is effectively free at this volume.
A flat per-listing fee regardless of token usage.
Only cache read tokens, since caching is the dominant cost driver.

questions.explanation: Input, output, and cache tokens are priced differently and must be modeled separately for an accurate per-listing cost breakdown. B, C, and D all oversimplify in ways that produce an inaccurate model.

questions.prompt: A new engineer argues the team can skip code review on the enrichment pipeline's application code since "the AI part is the risky part, not the plumbing." Question: What is the correct response? (Select ONE response.)

Only the prompt needs review; the surrounding code is low-risk by definition.
Code review is unnecessary once the enrichment evals pass.
Standard SDLC practices — code review, testing, version control — still apply to the application code around Claude; integrating an LLM doesn't replace engineering discipline.

questions.prompt: A single long-running session is reused across an entire shift to enrich listings from many unrelated sellers, and the team notices Claude increasingly referencing attributes from unrelated earlier listings. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Start a fresh session (or `/compact`) at natural task boundaries, such as between different sellers' batches, rather than accumulating unrelated context in one long session.
Ask the model to "forget earlier listings" at the start of each new one.
Increase the context window so more history fits without confusion.
Reduce temperature to prevent cross-referencing.

questions.explanation: Resetting at natural task boundaries prevents unrelated context from bleeding into new work. B is unreliable prompt-level mitigation; C doesn't address cross-contamination; D is an unrelated lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Most pull requests are small, routine changes (dependency bumps, formatting, minor refactors) where review is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per PR matter far more than catching rare, deeply subtle issues on every single diff. Question: Which model tier best fits the default review path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee nothing is ever missed.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token, regardless of review quality on flagged diffs.
The same tier used for the team's hardest architectural reviews, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity diffs, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as higher-risk.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity PRs fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged higher-risk cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and C overspend by default; B ignores review-quality fit entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs touch authentication, payment, or data-migration code, where the fast default model produces shallow, generic comments that miss real issues. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Route only the flagged high-risk PRs to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every PR to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Add many more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every PR.
Increase max_tokens for all PRs so comments can be longer.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged high-risk PRs to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume routine path. B, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The assistant currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review comment tone and the issues it flags shifted noticeably with no code change on Ashgrove's side. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Accept the drift — behavior changes across releases require no process.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix; D accepts avoidable risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Review comments need a consistent structure (issue, why it matters, suggested fix) but detailed prose instructions describing that structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask the model to restate the structure before commenting.
Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired comment structure.
Lower the temperature to zero.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A and D don't reliably fix structural consistency; B repeats a failed approach.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A pull request has a very large diff (2,000+ changed lines). The team wants a maximally thorough review comment set and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.
Output length has no measurable effect on latency.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very large diff leaves less room for a long comment set, and vice versa.
None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a large diff directly constrains available comment length and vice versa. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The review prompt currently places the specific diff text before the general review instructions and desired comment format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Placing instructions last always improves how carefully the model attends to them.
Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Reordering only affects cost, never comment consistency.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong first, forming a consistent, cacheable prefix; diff-specific content should come after as the varying part.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable diff content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and C misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the review assistant costs per pull request, but the team currently estimates cost only from average diff size. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Number of files touched only, regardless of token count.
Wall-clock review latency per PR, used as a cost proxy.
A flat cost assumption based on lines-changed count.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per PR, rather than an estimate from average diff size.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from diff size or unrelated proxies (A, B, C) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts a review comment must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample diff, and the eval fails intermittently even though the comments look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The eval needs a longer reference string to match against.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.
The model is broken and producing inconsistent answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A, B, and C misdiagnose the cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: PR payloads include full raw CI-tool output (every linter warning, every dependency-audit line) that bloats the review prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Increase max_tokens to accommodate the extra data.
Prune tool output to the relevant findings before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Summarize the CI output with a second Claude call before reviewing the diff.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant findings before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A, B, and D work around or add cost around a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: For very large diffs, the team notices review comments consistently miss issues in the middle files of the changeset while covering the first and last files well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to every file."
Alphabetize the changed files before reviewing.

Put a brief overview of the changeset's structure at the start of the input and organize per-file content under clear headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Switch to a model with an even larger context window.

questions.explanation: Placing a brief overview up front and organizing per-file detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A and B don't address the underlying attention pattern; D is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: A review comment confidently states that a function "already has a null check on this path," but on manual inspection the null check does not exist in the diff. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches a developer? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident claims — verify specific factual assertions (e.g., "already handled") against the actual diff rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Shorten review comments so there's less room for errors.
Increase the model's temperature so comments sound less confident.
Trust confident, fluent-sounding comments as evidence of correctness by default.

questions.explanation: Verifying specific factual claims against the actual diff catches confident-but-wrong comments that fluency alone would let through. B, C, and D don't address correctness.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: Detailed prose asking the model to "always output valid structured JSON with these exact fields" for machine-readable findings still produces occasional free-text preambles before the JSON. Question: What is the more reliable approach? (Select ONE response.)

Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`.
Increase max_tokens so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A, C, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Engineering leadership wants review comments fast and cheap for routine changes, while still catching subtle issues in the diffs that matter most.
questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a repository's broader codebase for context (related modules, prior patterns) before reviewing a diff, but worries the exploration will bloat the main review context with mostly-irrelevant detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

Skip broader-codebase context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Have a subagent perform the codebase scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main review step.
Increase the context window so the full related codebase always fits.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps codebase-scan bloat out of the main review context while still providing relevant findings. A and D reintroduce the bloat risk; B discards potentially useful context entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ashgrove Systems runs an internal code-review assistant that comments on pull requests across dozens of repositories, processing thousands of diffs per day. Multi-shot is always strictly better regardless of task simplicity.
Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. B and C are absolute claims that don't hold generally; D is false.

Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.
Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A new data analyst clones the team's dbt repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the repository root to take effect at all.
The new analyst needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review dbt model changes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The dbt models are too large for Claude Code to process.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and C would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

Post the entire raw output as one block on the status page instead of parsing it.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-output requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-lineage` custom command prints thousands of lines of table-lineage data, and engineers report Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so engineers scope the lineage query more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A and D narrow scope or capability but don't isolate output destination; C removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: An internal `/new-pipeline` skill is meant only to scaffold a new ETL job from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified an unrelated production config file. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Require engineers to commit their work before running any skill.
Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A mitigates damage rather than preventing it; B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team

questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a large, unfamiliar warehouse schema is structured before writing a new transformation, and worries that reading dozens of catalog entries will exhaust context before implementation begins. Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.
Read every catalog entry in one pass to be thorough.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A guesses instead of investigating; C doesn't share context between windows meaningfully; D floods context directly.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose schema-discovery output, but the engineer still needs to write the transformation in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A frees trivial space while losing standards; B describes behavior that doesn't exist; C discards findings.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls the data-catalog MCP tool, and writes a remediation report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the catalog tool returned valid schema data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The step between receiving the catalog tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Re-read the pipeline config again, since that's the earliest step.
Nothing — a wrong report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and catalog data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. B and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: A warehouse-query tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad credentials, wrong connection string) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Restart the CI runner and try again.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A, B, and C guess without diagnosis.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.

Build an MCP server exposing pipeline-status operations as tools, shared across the org.
Have each team paste warehouse credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code pipeline-status logic into each team's custom skill separately.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.

choices.text: A Claude Code Skill.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
An MCP tool, functionally identical to `search_tables`.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the warehouse-query MCP server should run as a local stdio process on each engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, C, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse connection password hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Rotate the password weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the password to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.
Base64-encode the password before committing it.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk; C doesn't remove the credential either.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected warehouse tools grant broader access (e.g., full `DROP TABLE` rights) than any actual analytics workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add a confirmation prompt before any destructive statement.
Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. B and C are detective/compensating controls; D accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: The data-engineering team at Cascade Logistics runs internal MCP servers exposing pipeline-status, data-catalog, and warehouse-query tools so that Claude Code sessions across the company can inspect ETL health and look up table schemas without engineers manually SSHing into anything.
questions.prompt: The team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific "weekly lineage report" workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused "check pipeline SLA status" capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

The one-off lineage report as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused SLA-status capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, B, and C force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 8.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The agent's harness needs to know when to stop executing tools and hand a finished review back to the paralegal who queued it. Question: What signal should the harness key off? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Whether `flag_risk` has been called at least once in the conversation.
A hard limit of five tool calls per contract, regardless of context.
Whether the most recent tool call succeeded without an error.
The `stop_reason` field on the response: continue the loop while it is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"`, stop at `"end_turn"`. Whether a specific tool was called (A), a fixed call cap (B), and error status (C) are all unreliable or secondary signals compared to the authoritative field.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: After `search_clause_library` returns matching precedent clauses, the harness needs the agent to keep reasoning about the contract with that information available. Question: What must the harness do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the corresponding `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.
Write the clause matches to a shared database and let the agent query it separately if needed.
Paste the clause matches into the system prompt so they persist for future contracts too.
Summarize the matches in a new user-authored message unrelated to the tool call.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent. Writing to a separate database (B) hides the result from the model; the system prompt (C) is the wrong place for turn-level data; a plain user message (D) breaks the expected tool-result linkage.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: Firm policy requires a licensed partner to approve any recommendation to reject a vendor contract outright. The system prompt states this rule clearly, but an audit finds the agent occasionally recommended outright rejection without triggering `request_partner_review`. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Repeat the rule near the end of the system prompt as well as the beginning.
Add several few-shot examples of the agent correctly escalating rejection recommendations.
Lower the temperature so the agent follows written policy more consistently.
Implement a hook that intercepts any final review output recommending rejection and blocks delivery unless `request_partner_review` was called first.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks delivery outright. Repeating the rule (A), few-shot examples (B), and lowering temperature (C) all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: The firm wants every review to begin with a mandatory `search_clause_library` call, with no exceptions, before any other tool runs. Question: What is the most reliable implementation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "search_clause_library"}` on the first request, then allow normal tool choice afterward.
State in the system prompt that clause-library lookup must always happen first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so some tool call is guaranteed.
Add several few-shot transcripts showing the clause lookup running first.

questions.explanation: Forcing tool choice on a specific tool guarantees it runs first; later turns proceed normally. A system-prompt statement (B) and `tool_choice: "any"` (C) don't guarantee which tool runs; few-shot examples (D) remain probabilistic.

questions.prompt: The agent currently has eleven tools, including several rarely used ones (billing lookup, e-signature routing, calendar scheduling) that have nothing to do with clause review. Tool selection has become inconsistent, with the agent occasionally calling the wrong tool for a straightforward review. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to reason about tool choice.
Add a system-prompt note ranking the eleven tools by importance.
Remove or scope out the tools unrelated to contract review from this agent's tool set.
Keep all eleven tools but rename them more descriptively.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core role directly reduces the candidate set the model must reason over. More reasoning tokens (A), a ranking note (B), and renaming (D) don't remove the actual capability bloat causing misselection.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. The agent has custom tools — `search_clause_library`, `flag_risk`, `request_partner_review`, and `redact_pii` — and its recommendations carry real legal and compliance weight, so tool-calling discipline and escalation behavior matter as much as the quality of its clause analysis.
questions.prompt: `redact_pii` currently returns the plain string `"failed"` whether the input document was missing, the redaction service timed out, or the user lacked permission to redact that document type. The agent responds inconsistently to each case. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add an automatic retry wrapper around every call.
Add a system-prompt note asking the agent to infer the failure type from context.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.
Increase the redaction service's timeout so failures occur less often.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent respond appropriately to each distinct failure. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures; asking the model to guess (B) is worse than the tool reporting it; a longer timeout (D) reduces frequency without fixing missing information.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Contract-Review Agent for a Legal Services Firm
questions.scenario_context: Meridian & Cole LLP, a mid-size legal services firm, has built an internal agent that reviews incoming vendor contracts before partners sign off. questions.prompt: When `search_clause_library` finds no precedent matching an unusual clause, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for a "system issue" and retrying the identical query. Question: What should change? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a system-prompt note explaining that this particular error usually means no precedent exists.
Have the agent call `flag_risk` automatically whenever this error occurs.
Return a successful response with an empty result set, reserving errors for genuine access failures.
Add a hook that silently ends the review whenever this error appears.

questions.explanation: "No precedent found" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty set. A prompt note (A) papers over the underlying conflation; auto-flagging (B) invents an unwarranted extra step; silently ending review (D) hides real signal.

questions.prompt: An associate proposes replacing the agent's judgment with a fixed sequence — always run `search_clause_library`, then `flag_risk`, then decide — arguing this makes review behavior predictable across all contract types. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit here? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Fixed sequences cannot invoke custom tools, only built-in ones.
Model-driven selection is always cheaper because it uses fewer reasoning tokens.
The harness technically cannot execute a fixed tool sequence.
Contract review is high-ambiguity; which clauses matter and what to check next depends on what earlier tool calls reveal, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity review where the next step depends on earlier findings is the core case for model-driven tool selection. The other options make unsupported technical claims about fixed sequences or cost.

questions.prompt: The firm wants to add `request_partner_review` but is deciding whether to give the main review agent that tool directly, or delegate escalation decisions to a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent. Escalating unnecessarily wastes a partner's billable time. Question: What is the strongest argument for a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A narrowly-scoped subagent can be given only the escalation tool and explicit escalation criteria, reducing the chance the main agent escalates unnecessarily while reasoning about unrelated clauses.
Subagents execute noticeably faster than tools called directly by the main agent.
The main agent's context window is too small to hold the escalation tool's schema.
Subagents are required whenever a tool has a real-world consequence.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the escalation tool and explicit criteria minimizes unnecessary escalations while the main agent reasons about unrelated clauses. B, C, and D are unsupported or overgeneralized claims.

Disable clause-library search and rely on the agent's general knowledge instead.
Increase `max_tokens` so responses can be longer.
Delegate clause-library exploration to a subagent that returns a distilled summary of relevant precedent, keeping the main agent's context focused on risk analysis.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: Customers watch a live typing indicator while Claude composes its answer, and the team wants the first words to appear as quickly as possible rather than waiting for the full response. Question: What technique best supports this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally as tokens arrive, reducing perceived latency.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the full response finishes generating sooner.
The Message Batches API, since it is designed for asynchronous chat delivery.
Polling a status endpoint every 500 milliseconds until the response is ready.

questions.explanation: Streaming renders output incrementally as tokens arrive, directly reducing perceived latency for a live typing indicator. B, C, and D don't address perceived latency the same way, and Batch/polling are the wrong tools for live chat.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: A nightly job re-summarizes the day's closed support chats for a quality dashboard. No customer is waiting on the result, and none of the summarization steps need a mid-request tool call. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API run across many parallel threads to finish quickly.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` minimized.
The synchronous Messages API paired with a smaller model to reduce cost.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or don't address the real cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Real-Time Streaming Support Chat Integration
questions.scenario_context: Northbay Retail runs a customer support chat widget where Claude answers order and shipping questions live while a customer is typing and waiting. The team is integrating streaming responses, tool calls for order lookups, and multi-vendor deployment considerations into the widget's backend.
questions.prompt: The team wants to add an "order-status lookup, verify against shipping carrier, retry if the carrier API times out" loop to the live chat flow, and considers running the whole loop through the Batch API to save cost. Question: Why won't this work as designed? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The Batch API's context window is too small for chat transcripts.
The 24-hour completion window makes retries structurally impossible.
The Batch API cannot execute a tool call mid-request and feed the result back to the model within a single request — required for this loop, and incompatible with a live customer waiting anyway.
The Batch API does not support system prompts.

questions.explanation: A retry/verify loop requires mid-request tool use, which the Batch API can't do — and it's the wrong fit for a live customer waiting regardless. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.prompt: Every chat turn sends the same 4,500-token support policy and tone guidelines, followed by the specific customer message, which varies per turn. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many turns? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the policy guidelines into a few-shot example block instead.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of answer quality.
Place the stable policy and tone guidelines first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying customer message last.
Truncate the policy guidelines to reduce token count.

questions.explanation: Placing stable content first with caching enabled and variable content last maximizes cache hits, cutting both latency and cost. A, B, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The order-lookup tool's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 4% of chat turns produce malformed JSON that breaks the widget's rendering logic. Question: What is the most reliable fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Ask for YAML output instead, since it tolerates formatting drift better.
Define a `submit_order_lookup` tool whose input schema matches the needed structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to fix common syntax issues before parsing.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the parsing failure class outright. A, C, and D are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated.

Question: What should the team conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Schema compliance guarantees syntax, not semantics — add a validation step that checks the displayed estimate against the carrier status on top of schema compliance.
`max_tokens` is too low, truncating output mid-generation.
The schema needs stricter date types to fix this.
Abandon tool use and return to free-text order lookups with manual review.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step is needed to catch cross-field contradictions. B, C, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.prompt: Some customers attach a photo of a damaged product, and the pipeline currently sends only an OCR-extracted caption of the image to Claude. Answers about visible damage are poor when the caption is generic or missing detail. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a larger model, since bigger models are always better at working from vague captions.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model can reason harder about the caption.
Send the photo itself as an image content block alongside the customer's message, using Claude's native vision input instead of relying solely on the caption.
Reject photo attachments from the chat flow entirely.

questions.explanation: Sending the photo directly as a vision content block bypasses a lossy, generic caption entirely. A and B don't address the actual data bottleneck; D discards otherwise-useful attachments.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Optimizing a Multilingual Content-Moderation Service
questions.scenario_context: Vantora Media runs a content-moderation service that screens user-submitted comments across a dozen languages for policy violations before publication, processing several million comments per day. The team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to keep latency, cost, and moderation consistency within target.
questions.prompt: Most submitted comments are short and moderation is a simple binary classification. Latency and per-comment cost matter far more than handling rare, highly ambiguous edge cases perfectly. Question: Which model tier best fits the default moderation path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee accuracy on every comment.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity classification, reserving a higher tier only for comments flagged as ambiguous.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token, regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency across teams.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity classification fits a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged ambiguous cases. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Optimizing a Multilingual Content-Moderation Service
questions.scenario_context: Vantora Media runs a content-moderation service that screens user-submitted comments across a dozen languages for policy violations before publication, processing several million comments per day. The team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to keep latency, cost, and moderation consistency within target.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of comments require nuanced judgment (satire versus genuine harassment, coded language, cultural context) where the fast default model produces shallow or inconsistent verdicts. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` for every comment to give more room to reason.
Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every comment.
Switch every comment to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Route only the flagged ambiguous comments to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged ambiguous cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Optimizing a Multilingual Content-Moderation Service
questions.scenario_context: Vantora Media runs a content-moderation service that screens user-submitted comments across a dozen languages for policy violations before publication, processing several million comments per day. The team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to keep latency, cost, and moderation consistency within target.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, moderation verdicts shifted noticeably in borderline cases with no code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Roll back permanently to the oldest available model version.
Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and needs no process.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A, B, and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

Output length has no effect on latency.

Alphabetize comments before moderation.
Put a brief thread overview at the start of the input and organize the detailed comments under clear section markers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims against the source comment rather than accepting fluency as correctness.

Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.

Load the entire comment history directly into the main prompt every time.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new QA hire clones the team's test-automation repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established bug-report conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The new hire needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new hire cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to triage newly flaky tests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.
The flaky-test list is too large for Claude Code to process.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.
