You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A downstream dashboard parses `/triage-flaky` output with regex to file tickets automatically, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Run with `--output-format json` and a defined schema for the triage findings, producing machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw output as a single ticket comment instead of parsing it.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, B, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-parsing requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Skills and Commands for a QA Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The `/gen-test-plan` command prints thousands of lines of exploratory code-reading output while building context on the feature under test, and QA engineers report Claude's answers about their actual follow-up questions get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so engineers scope the exploration more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose exploration runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates the command's verbose exploration in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A and D scope or restrict differently but don't isolate output; C removes useful functionality.

You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/draft-bug-report` Skill is meant only to create a formatted markdown file from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated test fixtures. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the Skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Add a warning in the Skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require engineers to commit their work before running any Skill.
Convert the Skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the Skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about commands.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). questions.prompt: A QA engineer needs to understand how a flaky integration test's setup fixtures interact across a large, unfamiliar test suite before proposing a fix, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before the fix itself is written. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Read every file in the test suite in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer fixture behavior from file names.
Split the investigation across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for the fix itself. B floods context directly; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't meaningfully share context between windows.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). You support this team's configuration, CI usage, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose fixture-exploration output, but the engineer still needs to implement the fix in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A describes behavior that doesn't exist; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D discards findings.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a test-config file, calls `/triage-flaky`'s underlying analysis, and writes a bug report produces a wrong root-cause conclusion. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the triage analysis returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — a wrong conclusion with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

The step between receiving the valid triage data and producing the final conclusion — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection used to read the test-config file, since that's the earliest step.
Re-read the test-config file again, since that's the earliest step.

questions.explanation: Since the config and triage data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about — that's where the trace should focus next. A, C, and D re-check already-verified steps or skip diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A test-runner integration fails intermittently, and the QA team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad flags, wrong exit-code parsing) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual command invocation and its output) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was run and returned.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was run and returned, before assuming which side is at fault. A, C, and D guess without diagnosis.

Ask each engineer to manually re-type the plan format when needed.

questions.prompt: The team's `.claude/settings.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a bug-tracker API token hardcoded directly in a hook script referenced by the config. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Move the settings file to a private repository instead.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that `/triage-flaky`'s `allowed-tools` configuration grants it broader shell access (including the ability to delete test artifacts) than the triage workflow actually requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.
Scope `allowed-tools` down to only the operations the triage workflow actually requires, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.
Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A, B, and D are detective/compensating controls or accept unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Software's QA team has adopted Claude Code for writing test plans, triaging flaky tests, and drafting bug reports, and has built a set of team-specific Skills and slash commands (`/triage-flaky`, `/draft-bug-report`, `/gen-test-plan`). questions.prompt: The QA team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific bug-report formatting workflow used only by QA, versus a widely-reused test-environment-health-check capability needed by every engineering team at Cascade. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The one-off bug-report workflow as a Skill or command scoped to the QA team; the widely-reused health-check capability as a centrally maintained plugin/shared tool available to every consuming team.
Both as one-off Skills, since Skills are always team-specific.
Both as centrally maintained plugins, since that is the correct choice for any capability.
Both as ad hoc shell scripts, since that requires the least setup.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — a scoped Skill/command for the one-off QA workflow, a centrally maintained plugin for the widely shared health-check — is the correct architecture. B, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile.

questions.prompt: The QA lead wants Claude Code sessions to automatically run the project's linter and block a commit if it fails, without relying on Claude choosing to run the linter on its own. Question: What is the correct mechanism? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: A hook bound to the relevant lifecycle event (e.g., before commit) that runs the linter deterministically and blocks the action on failure.
A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to always lint before committing.
A few-shot example showing a session running the linter before committing.
A Skill description mentioning that linting is recommended.

questions.prompt: A `/draft-bug-report` command frequently produces reports with an inconsistent severity field — sometimes "High," sometimes "P1," sometimes "critical" — because the command's prompt only says to "assign an appropriate severity." choices.text: Lower the temperature used for the command.

Constrain the severity field with an explicit enumerated set of allowed values (e.g., via schema-constrained output or an explicit list in the instructions), rather than leaving it to free-text judgment.
Ask engineers to manually correct the severity field after generation.
Remove the severity field from bug reports entirely.

questions.explanation: Constraining the severity field to an explicit enumerated set (ideally via schema-constrained output) removes the ambiguity causing inconsistent labels. A, C, and D don't address the root cause of the inconsistency. --- *End of Practice Exam 9.*

questions.scenario_context: NimbusHost operates virtual machines and managed containers for thousands of customers. The platform team is building "Aegis," an internal incident-response agent built on the Claude Agent SDK, with custom tools including `check_node_status`, `restart_container`, `scale_replica_pool`, `open_customer_incident`, and `escalate_to_oncall`. Several of these tools are destructive or customer-visible, so how tool access is granted and enforced matters as much as Aegis's reasoning quality.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants Aegis's tool-use loop to keep executing tools and returning results until Claude has no further tool calls to make. What should the loop's continue/stop decision key off?

choices.text: The `stop_reason` value returned with each response: continue while it equals `tool_use`, stop once it becomes `end_turn`.
A hard limit of 5 tool calls per session, regardless of content.
Scanning the assistant's text for phrases like "issue resolved."
Whether the most recent tool call took longer than 2 seconds to return.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (C) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; call duration (D) doesn't indicate completion.

questions.prompt: After `restart_container` executes, what must the client code do so Aegis can keep reasoning correctly about the incident?

choices.text: Summarize the restart outcome into a new system prompt for the next turn.
Append a `tool_result` content block tagged with the originating `tool_use_id`, then resend the full conversation to the model.
Write the outcome to the incident ticket only, since Aegis will infer success from context.
End the current turn and start a fresh conversation containing just the result.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use_id`, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data; C keeps the result from the model entirely; D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Policy requires human approval before `restart_container` runs on any production load-balancer node. The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show occasional unapproved restarts on those nodes anyway. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: A hook that intercepts `restart_container` calls and blocks any targeting a production load-balancer node absent a recorded approval.
Restate the approval requirement at both the top and bottom of the system prompt.
Add few-shot examples showing Aegis correctly requesting approval first.
Reduce the model's temperature so Aegis follows the stated policy more literally.

questions.explanation: A safety-critical rule affecting customer-facing infrastructure needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. B, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

Set `tool_choice` to force the `check_node_status` tool specifically on the first request, then use normal tool choice for subsequent turns.
Add a few-shot transcript demonstrating `check_node_status` called first.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (D) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. A and C are probabilistic.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Batch Invoice-Extraction Pipeline for a Logistics Company
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Logistics runs a document-intelligence pipeline that extracts structured line-item and total data from freight invoices and bills of lading. The pipeline handles two flows: an overnight batch job processing tens of thousands of scanned invoices with no one waiting, and an interactive lookup used by customer-service reps who upload a single invoice and wait on the result.
questions.prompt: The overnight batch job processes 25,000 freight invoices with no user waiting on the result, and no step requires Claude to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why?

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API with the smallest available model, to minimize cost.
The synchronous Messages API run across many parallel threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume processing at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` set to the minimum needed.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. B doesn't reduce per-token cost; A and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Batch Invoice-Extraction Pipeline for a Logistics Company
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Logistics runs a document-intelligence pipeline that extracts structured line-item and total data from freight invoices and bills of lading. The pipeline handles two flows: an overnight batch job processing tens of thousands of scanned invoices with no one waiting, and an interactive lookup used by customer-service reps who upload a single invoice and wait on the result.
questions.prompt: An engineer wants to add an iterative "extract, validate against schema, retry failed fields" loop to improve accuracy, and proposes running the whole loop through the Batch API for its cost savings. Question: Why won't this work as designed?

choices.text: The Batch API cannot execute a mid-request validation tool call and feed results back to the model within a single request — required for this iterative loop.
The Batch API doesn't support system prompts.
The 24-hour completion window makes any retry logic impossible.
The Batch API's context window is too small for freight-invoice-length documents.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. B, C, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.prompt: The interactive single-invoice flow shows the customer-service rep a real-time progress indicator while Claude processes the upload. Question: What technique best supports this user experience?

choices.text: The Batch API, since it is designed for real-time feedback.
Increasing `max_tokens` so the full response arrives sooner.
Streaming, so the UI can render output incrementally and reduce perceived latency.
Polling the Batch API's status endpoint once per second.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. A is the wrong API for this use case; B and D don't address perceived latency.

questions.scenario_context: Cascade Logistics runs a document-intelligence pipeline that extracts structured line-item and total data from freight invoices and bills of lading. The pipeline handles two flows: an overnight batch job processing tens of thousands of scanned invoices with no one waiting, and an interactive lookup used by customer-service reps who upload a single invoice and wait on the result.
questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 6,000-token extraction instructions and field-schema reference, followed by the specific invoice text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests?

choices.text: Move the schema reference into a few-shot example block instead.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of extraction quality.
Place the stable extraction instructions and schema reference first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying invoice text last.
Truncate the schema reference to save tokens.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and D either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The extraction schema currently requires a `discount_amount` field on every invoice. Many invoices have no discount, and the model has started inventing small values rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this?

choices.text: Remove the field from the schema entirely.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent values.
Make `discount_amount` nullable so its absence can be reported truthfully.
Lower the temperature to reduce invented values.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. B and D rely on probabilistic compliance or lose data; A removes the field's value entirely.

questions.prompt: Two credible extraction passes on the same invoice disagree: one reads the total as $6,140.00, the other as $6,140.50, and there's no way to tell which is correct from context alone. Question: What should the pipeline do?

choices.text: Average the two values.
Discard the invoice entirely since the data is unreliable.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source rather than silently picking one.
Always trust whichever extraction pass ran first.

questions.explanation: Conflicting extractions with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard information or guess.

questions.prompt: The extraction step's JSON output occasionally fails to parse — about 3% of runs produce malformed JSON that crashes the downstream loader. Question: What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to fix common syntax issues before parsing.
Ask for YAML output instead, since it's more forgiving of formatting drift.
Define a `submit_extraction` tool whose input schema matches the extraction structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. A and B are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; C swaps one fragile text format for another.

questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, extraction output always parses successfully, but some extracted line-item amounts don't sum to the stated invoice total. Question: What should you conclude and do?

choices.text: The schema needs stricter numeric types to fix this.
`max_tokens` is too low, truncating output mid-generation.
Abandon tool use and return to free-text extraction with human review.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic errors — add a validation step that checks totals against line-item sums on top of schema compliance.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking totals against line items) is needed on top. A, B, and C misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.prompt: A subset of incoming invoices are scanned images with no text layer. The pipeline currently sends only OCR-extracted text to Claude, and quality is poor on documents with damaged OCR output. Question: What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Reject scanned invoices from the pipeline entirely.
Send the invoice image itself as a content block alongside the extraction instructions, using Claude's native vision input instead of relying solely on OCR text.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model can work harder on the degraded OCR text.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models are always better at reading noisy text.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged documents. C and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable documents.

questions.prompt: The pipeline needs to run extraction on several sections of a long bill of lading concurrently to keep latency reasonable, rather than processing sections one at a time. Question: What must the integration layer support to do this?

choices.text: Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple API calls can be in flight at once without blocking on each other.
Streaming, since only streaming supports concurrency.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to run more than one request at a time.
A single request with all sections concatenated, since Claude parallelizes internally.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. B, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

Bedrock requires a completely different prompting approach and schema design.
Batch processing is unavailable on all third-party vendor integrations.

questions.scenario_context: Ledgerline Analytics generates automated narrative commentary for corporate finance teams — quarterly variance write-ups, budget-vs-actual summaries, and consolidated multi-entity reports. Most reports are short and routine; a smaller fraction involve complex multi-entity consolidations that require careful cross-referencing. The team is tuning model selection, prompt structure, and context handling to hit accuracy, cost, and latency targets.
questions.prompt: Most reports are short, routine variance write-ups, and the task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per report matter far more than handling rare, highly complex consolidations well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every report.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning work, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity tasks, reserving a higher tier only for reports flagged as complex.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend or ignore task fit; C is an unrelated consideration.

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every report.
Route only the flagged complex reports to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.
Switch every report to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all reports regardless of complexity.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, C, and D apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

Ask the model to restate the structure before drafting the report.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; B and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong first (system prompt or start of the turn) to form a consistent, cacheable prefix; report-specific data should come after as the varying part.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a longer reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Prune the source data to the relevant fields before it enters the prompt, rather than passing raw exports.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before drafting the report.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. A and B work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole document."

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.
Alphabetize the source sections before drafting.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and D don't address the underlying attention pattern.

Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key figures and claims against the source data rather than accepting fluency as correctness.
Shorten the report so there's less room for errors.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source data catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and D don't address correctness.

Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main report-drafting step.

The choice has no effect on cost or latency.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code Governance for a Growing Platform Org
questions.scenario_context: Fenwick Platform Engineering supports roughly 90 engineers using Claude Code across dozens of repositories, alongside internal MCP servers for ticketing, deployment status, and internal documentation. As adoption grows, the platform team owns team-wide configuration, CI integration, and security governance for how Claude Code and MCP are used across the org.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established coding conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: `CLAUDE.md` requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level `CLAUDE.md` never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how `CLAUDE.md` loading actually works.

questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's `CLAUDE.md` is malformed.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and C would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-deps` custom command prints thousands of lines of dependency-graph data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

`argument-hint`, so developers scope the analysis more narrowly.
Removing the command entirely.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; C removes useful functionality.

questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-service` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. B floods context directly; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a config file, calls an internal MCP tool, and writes a report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Order-Fulfillment Automation Agent for an E-Commerce Retailer
questions.scenario_context: You are building an internal fulfillment agent for Cascade Outfitters, a mid-size e-commerce retailer selling outdoor gear, using the Claude Agent SDK. It has custom tools (`check_inventory`, `reserve_stock`, `create_shipping_label`, `cancel_order`, `notify_customer`, `escalate_to_ops`) and resolves order exceptions — backorders, address problems, fraud holds — that the automated fulfillment system can't handle on its own.
questions.prompt: The fulfillment agent's tool-use loop must decide when to stop executing tools and hand control back to the human ops queue. What should drive that decision?

choices.text: Whether the last tool result contains the word "complete."
A hard limit of five tool calls per order.
Whether the model's response text is longer than 200 tokens.
The `stop_reason` field: keep executing tools while it equals `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (A) are unreliable; a fixed cap (B) is a backstop, not a primary mechanism; response length (C) says nothing about completion.

questions.prompt: After `reserve_stock` runs and returns a result, what must the integration code do so the agent can reason correctly on the next turn?

choices.text: Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` id and send the full updated conversation back to the model.
Write the result to an order log and let the next user message summarize it.
Inject the result directly into the system prompt for the rest of the session.
Start a new conversation seeded with just the result.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. B keeps the result from the model entirely. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Ops policy requires that `cancel_order` never be called on any order already marked "shipped." The system prompt states this clearly, but logs show occasional violations. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the rule at both the start and end of the system prompt.
Add few-shot examples of the agent correctly refusing to cancel shipped orders.
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated policy more consistently.
Implement a hook that intercepts `cancel_order` calls and blocks any targeting an order already marked shipped.

questions.explanation: A policy with real financial/operational consequences needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that blocks the call outright. A, B, and C all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_exception"}` on the first request, then use normal tool choice afterward.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (B) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. A and C are probabilistic.

Increase the warehouse system's timeout so failures become rarer.

questions.scenario_context: You maintain Fenwick Analytics, a SaaS platform that routes Claude requests through the direct Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Vertex AI depending on each enterprise customer's data-residency and procurement requirements. The platform handles both interactive ticket classification for live dashboards and large overnight batch jobs.
questions.prompt: An overnight job classifies 50,000 support tickets with no user waiting on the result and no step that needs the model to call a tool mid-request. Question: Which API best fits, and why? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The synchronous Messages API run in parallel across many threads, to finish as fast as possible.
The Message Batches API — latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work at reduced cost.
The synchronous Messages API with a smaller model to reduce cost.
The synchronous Messages API with `max_tokens` reduced to the minimum.

questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant, non-blocking, high-volume work with no mid-request tool calls is exactly the Batch API's fit, at reduced cost versus synchronous calls. A doesn't reduce per-token cost; C and D risk quality or truncate output without addressing the actual cost lever.

The 24-hour window makes any retry logic impossible.
The Batch API cannot execute a validation tool call mid-request and feed results back to the model within a single request — required for this iterative loop.
The Batch API's context window is too small for ticket-length threads.

questions.explanation: An iterative validate-and-retry loop is inherently multi-turn tool use, which the Batch API cannot support mid-request. A, B, and D misidentify the actual limitation.

questions.explanation: Streaming supports incremental rendering, reducing perceived latency for real-time progress UIs. B is the wrong API for this use case; C and D don't address perceived latency.

questions.prompt: Every request sends the same 5,000-token classification taxonomy, followed by the specific ticket text, which varies per request. Question: What optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost across many requests? (Select ONE response.)

Truncate the taxonomy to save tokens.
Place the stable taxonomy first, enable prompt caching, and put the varying ticket text last.

questions.explanation: Only a shared prefix is cacheable; placing stable content first and variable content last maximizes cache hits, reducing both latency and cost. A, B, and C either break the cacheable prefix or degrade quality without addressing caching.

questions.prompt: The classification schema currently requires an `urgency_reason` field on every ticket. Many tickets have no clear urgency driver, and the model has started inventing plausible-sounding reasons rather than reporting none. Question: What schema change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Remove the field from the schema entirely.
Make `urgency_reason` nullable so its absence can be reported truthfully.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to invent values.
Lower the temperature to reduce invented values.

questions.explanation: Making the field nullable lets the model truthfully report a genuine absence instead of inventing a value to satisfy a required field. A discards the field's value entirely; C and D rely on probabilistic compliance rather than a structural fix.

Discard the ticket entirely since the data is unreliable.
Flag the field for human review with both candidate values and their source rather than silently picking one.
Always trust the first classification pass.

questions.explanation: Conflicting classifications with no way to resolve them from context should be surfaced for human review with both candidates and sources, not resolved arbitrarily. A, B, and D all discard information or guess.

choices.text: Define a `submit_classification` tool whose input schema matches the classification structure, and read the data from the structured `tool_use` block instead of parsing free text.
Wrap the parse in a try/catch and retry with "valid JSON only" appended to the prompt.
Add a JSON-repair library to fix common syntax issues before parsing.
Ask for YAML output instead, since it's more forgiving of formatting drift.

questions.explanation: Tool-use with a matching input schema guarantees structurally valid output, eliminating the JSON-in-text parsing failure class outright. B and C are recovery layers for a problem that can be eliminated; D swaps one fragile text format for another.

questions.prompt: Since switching to strict schema-constrained tool use, classification output always parses successfully, but some extracted line-item totals don't sum to the stated ticket-refund amount. Question: What should you conclude and do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The schema needs stricter numeric types to fix this.
`max_tokens` is too low, truncating output mid-generation.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic errors — add a validation step that checks totals against line-item sums on top of schema compliance.
Abandon tool use and return to free-text extraction with human review.

questions.explanation: Schema validity guarantees syntax, not semantics; a separate validation step (checking totals against line items) is needed on top. A, B, and D misdiagnose or abandon a working mechanism.

questions.prompt: A subset of incoming tickets include scanned receipt images with no text layer. The pipeline currently sends only OCR-extracted text to Claude, and quality is poor on receipts with damaged OCR output. Question: What is the most direct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Reject tickets with scanned receipts from the pipeline entirely.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model can work harder on the degraded OCR text.
Send the receipt image itself as a content block alongside the classification instructions, using Claude's native vision input instead of relying solely on OCR text.
Switch to a larger model, since bigger models are always better at reading noisy text.

questions.explanation: Sending the image directly as a vision content block bypasses lossy OCR entirely for damaged documents. B and D don't address the actual data-quality bottleneck; A discards otherwise-processable tickets.

Async/concurrent request handling, so multiple API calls can be in flight at once without blocking on each other.
The Batch API, since it's the only way to run more than one request at a time.
A single request with all five batches concatenated, since Claude parallelizes internally.

questions.explanation: Concurrent tool/API calls require async/non-blocking request handling in the integration layer. A, C, and D misstate how concurrency is actually achieved.

Batch processing is unavailable on all third-party vendor integrations.

Handle the thinking content block as distinct from the final answer text, typically preserving it appropriately across the multi-turn tool-use conversation.
Convert thinking output into a separate tool call.

Only output tokens, since input is effectively free.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most tickets are short and the triage task is simple and extremely high-volume. Latency and cost per ticket matter far more than handling rare, highly complex edge cases well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every ticket.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity tasks, reserving a higher tier only for tickets flagged as complex.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and B overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: A small fraction of tickets require multi-step reasoning (tracing a multi-account billing dispute) where the fast default model produces shallow triage notes. Question: What is the most targeted fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every ticket.
Switch every ticket to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all tickets.
Route only the flagged complex tickets to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex cases to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, triage categories and tone shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and D are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: Triage notes need a consistent structure (category, priority, suggested queue) but detailed prose instructions describing the structure haven't produced consistent output. Question: What technique is most likely to help? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Write an even longer, more detailed prose description of the structure.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.
Lower the temperature to zero.
Ask the model to restate the structure before triaging.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; C and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: A ticket thread is very long (50+ messages). The team wants maximally detailed triage notes and considers requesting a very long output to match. Question: What tradeoff must they account for? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.
Output length has no effect on latency.
Input and output share the same context-window budget, so a very long input leaves less room for a long output, and vice versa.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so long input directly constrains available output length and vice versa. A, B, and D misstate this relationship.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The triage prompt currently places the specific ticket text before the general triage instructions and desired format in every request. Question: Why might reordering improve both consistency and cacheability? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Order has no effect on either consistency or caching.
Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or placed first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; ticket-specific content should come after as the varying part.
Placing instructions last always improves model attention.
Reordering only affects cost, never consistency.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improves consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, C, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Finance wants to know exactly how much the triage service costs per ticket, but the team currently estimates cost only from average prompt length. Question: What should be instrumented instead? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Wall-clock latency per ticket, used as a cost proxy.
Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per ticket, rather than an estimate from average length.
Number of API calls only, regardless of token count.
A flat cost assumption based on ticket character count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per ticket gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average length or unrelated proxies (A, C, D) don't.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. Cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model tier selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: An engineer writes an automated eval that asserts the triage output must exactly match a fixed reference string for a sample ticket, and the eval fails intermittently even though the notes look correct on manual review. Question: What is the most likely issue with the eval design? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Model Tiering for a High-Volume Ticket-Triage Service
questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: Ticket payloads include full raw metadata dumps (every field of every message) that bloat the prompt with mostly-irrelevant data, slowing the pipeline and increasing cost. Question: What is the best fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Prune tool/data output to the relevant fields before they enter the prompt, rather than passing raw dumps.
Increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the extra data.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the bloat matters less.
Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before triaging.

questions.explanation: Pruning to relevant fields before data enters the prompt removes the actual bloat at its source. B and C work around the symptom without reducing waste; D adds cost and complexity for a problem solvable by simple filtering.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: For very long ticket threads, the team notices triage notes consistently miss details from the middle of the conversation while capturing the opening and closing messages well. Question: What is the most effective mitigation? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window.
Add an instruction telling the model to "pay equal attention to the whole conversation."
Alphabetize the messages before triaging.

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.prompt: A triage note confidently states a resolution that, on manual review, never actually happened in the ticket thread. Question: What practice would most help catch this class of error before it reaches the dashboard? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Trust confident, fluent-sounding output as evidence of correctness by default.
Increase the model's temperature so answers sound less confident.
Shorten the note so there's less room for errors.
Apply defensive parsing and skepticism toward confident output — verify key claims (e.g., "resolution" fields) against the source thread rather than accepting fluency as correctness.

questions.explanation: Verifying key claims against the source thread catches confident-but-wrong output that fluency alone would let through. A is the failure mode itself; B and C don't address correctness.

Use tool-use/schema-constrained output so the structure is enforced by the API mechanism rather than requested through prose.
Post-process every response to strip text before the first `{`.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's room for both the preamble and the JSON.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool-use output is enforced by the API mechanism, unlike prose requests that can still drift. A and C are workarounds for a problem that can be structurally eliminated; D doesn't address the preamble issue.

questions.scenario_context: You run Solstice Support, a customer-support software vendor whose triage service classifies and routes hundreds of thousands of tickets per day across many client accounts. questions.prompt: The team wants to add an exploratory step that scans a customer account's full ticket history for context before triaging the current ticket, but worries the exploration will bloat the main context with mostly-irrelevant historical detail. Question: What is the best structural approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Load the entire ticket history directly into the main prompt every time.
Have a subagent perform the historical scan in an isolated context and return only a distilled, relevant summary to the main triage step.
Skip historical context entirely to avoid the bloat risk.
Increase the context window so the full history always fits.

questions.explanation: An isolated subagent scan returning a distilled summary keeps historical bloat out of the main context while still providing relevant findings. A and D reintroduce the bloat risk; C discards potentially useful context entirely.

Zero-shot is required whenever latency matters at all.
The choice has no effect on cost or latency.
For a simple, well-understood, high-volume task, zero-shot may be sufficient and cheaper; multi-shot earns its extra token cost on tasks needing specific formatting or edge-case consistency.

questions.explanation: Task simplicity and volume should drive the zero-shot-vs-multi-shot tradeoff; multi-shot earns its cost on tasks needing format/edge-case consistency, which a simple high-volume task may not need. A and B are absolute claims that don't hold generally; C is false.

Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. A, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the mobile team's repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established Swift and Kotlin style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and C misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline

questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review mobile pull requests and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. B, C, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's PR review output with regex to post inline comments, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. B, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-native-deps` custom command prints thousands of lines of dependency-graph data, and developers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: `context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
`allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
`argument-hint`, so developers scope the analysis more narrowly.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. B restricts capability, not output destination; C narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-screen` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. B is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how push-notification handling flows across a large, unfamiliar mobile codebase before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Read every file in the codebase in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the architecture from directory names.
Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. A floods context directly; B guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output about the crash-reporting integration, but the engineer still needs to implement the change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. A discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a build-config file, calls an internal MCP tool for crash data, and writes a triage report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid crash data. Question: Where should debugging focus next? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.
Just the final error message, since the human can re-investigate from there.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; B skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code and MCP for a Mobile App Team's CI Pipeline
questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A build-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. B and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.prompt: The internal crash-reporting system needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole mobile engineering org, not just one team, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming app. Question: What is the best approach? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Have each team paste crash-reporting API credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Build an MCP server exposing crash-reporting operations as tools, shared across the org and maintained centrally by the platform team.
Hard-code crash-reporting logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Ask each engineer to curl the crash-reporting API manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, C, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.prompt: An MCP server for build-status exposes both a `check_build` tool and a way for agents to see what recent builds exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: An MCP tool, functionally identical to `check_build`.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
A Claude Code Skill.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. A, B, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the app-store-metadata MCP server should run as a local stdio process per developer machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and C are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the mobile repository, currently has an app-store-metadata API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${APP_STORE_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.
Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. B is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; C and D don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full crash-log deletion rights) than any actual mobile engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any deletion.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario_context: You support Trailmark Mobile's iOS and Android engineering team's use of Claude Code and a set of internal MCP servers (build-status, crash-reporting, app-store-metadata). You're responsible for team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific release-notes generator used by a single small mobile squad, versus a widely-reused build-status-checking capability needed by every agent across the org. Question: How should each be built? (Select ONE response.)

choices.text: The one-off release-notes generator as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused build-status capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. B, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 11.*
