questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: An engineer builds a tool-execution loop for the research agent that must keep calling tools and returning results until Claude has nothing more to do on its own. What should the loop check to decide when to stop?

choices.text: Continue while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, and stop once it becomes `"end_turn"`.
Stop as soon as `find_contacts` has been called once.
Stop after a fixed 5-second timer regardless of tool calls.
Stop when the response text contains the word "brief."

questions.explanation: The tool-use loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it's `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Text-based signals (D) are unreliable; a single-call stop (B) or fixed timer (C) don't reflect what Claude actually needs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: After `pull_funding_data` runs, what must the integration code do so Claude can correctly reason about the result on the next turn?

choices.text: Insert the raw funding data directly into a new system prompt for the remainder of the session.
Append a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID to the conversation and resend the full conversation to the model.
Store the funding data in the CRM database only; the model doesn't need to see it directly.
Start a new session and paste a summary of the funding data as the first user message.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the full conversation resent so the model can incorporate the result. C keeps the result from the model entirely. A misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D discards conversational state unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Sales Research Agent with Subagents for a B2B SaaS Company
questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: Meridian's policy requires that contacts from EU-based companies never be surfaced with personal emails unless a consent flag is set. The rule is stated clearly in the system prompt, but logs show occasional violations. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the rule at both the start and end of the system prompt.
Add a hook that intercepts `find_contacts` output and redacts personal emails for EU contacts lacking a consent flag.
Add few-shot examples of correctly redacting EU contacts.
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the stated policy more consistently.

questions.explanation: A compliance-critical rule needs deterministic enforcement via a hook that redacts the data outright. A, C, and D all remain probabilistic prompt compliance, which is exactly what's failing at the observed rate.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The team wants `classify_account_tier` to always run first, with no exceptions, before any other tool. Question: What is the most reliable implementation?

choices.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_account_tier"}` on the first request, then use normal tool choice afterward.
State in the system prompt that `classify_account_tier` must always run first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so a tool call is guaranteed.
Add several few-shot examples showing the classification tool called first.

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice on a specific tool guarantees that tool runs first; later turns proceed normally. `tool_choice: "any"` (C) guarantees some tool call, but not which one. B and D are probabilistic.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: The research agent has grown to 14 tools, including several rarely-used ones (expense-report lookup, internal HR directory) unrelated to sales research. Tool selection has become unreliable. Question: What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to reason about which tool to pick.
Add a system prompt note listing which tools are "primary," while keeping all 14 available.
Add more few-shot examples showing correct tool selection among all 14 tools.
Remove or scope out the tools unrelated to the agent's core sales-research role.

questions.explanation: Removing tools unrelated to the agent's core role directly reduces the candidate set the agent must reason over, improving selection reliability. B adds prompt overhead without removing the actual capability bloat. A and C don't address the root cause.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. Before a call, the agent pulls company background, funding signals, and contact details using tools like `lookup_company`, `pull_funding_data`, `find_contacts`, and `draft_call_brief`, and can delegate parts of the research to subagents.
questions.prompt: `find_contacts` currently returns the string `"Error"` for every possible failure — invalid domain, permission denied, or directory-service timeout. The agent responds inconsistently to each. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Wrap every call in an automatic retry policy.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to infer the failure type from context.
Return structured error metadata: an error category, a retryable flag, and a human-readable description.
Increase the directory service's timeout so failures become rarer.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, description) lets the agent decide how to respond appropriately. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on non-retryable failures. Asking the model to guess (B) is strictly worse than the tool reporting it. D reduces frequency without fixing the missing information.

questions.scenario_context: Meridian CRM is building an internal sales research agent for its account executives. questions.prompt: When `find_contacts` finds no matching contacts at a target account, it currently returns an error. The agent responds by apologizing for "technical difficulties" and retrying the same query. What should change?

choices.text: Have the agent call `lookup_company` first to check whether contacts should exist.
Add a hook that suppresses the error and ends the conversation.
Return a successful response with an empty result set, reserving errors for actual access failures.
Add a system prompt note explaining that this error usually means no contacts matched.

questions.explanation: "No matching contacts" is a valid empty result, not a failure — return success with an empty set. B hides real signal. A invents an unnecessary extra step. D patches symptoms while the underlying success/error conflation remains.

questions.prompt: An engineer proposes replacing the agent's reasoning with a fixed sequence: always call `lookup_company`, then `pull_funding_data`, then `find_contacts`. They argue this makes behavior predictable. Question: Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit for account research?

choices.text: Model-driven selection is always cheaper since it skips unnecessary reasoning tokens.
The Claude Agent SDK technically cannot run fixed tool sequences.
Research needs vary by account and depend on intermediate findings, which a fixed sequence can't adapt to.
Fixed sequences cannot invoke custom tools, only built-in ones.

questions.explanation: High-ambiguity research where the right tools/order depend on intermediate findings is the core case for model-driven selection. A, B, and D are false or unsupported claims about the technology.

Sending outreach has real cost (reaching a real prospect) and should only happen under specific approval criteria. Question: What is the strongest argument for a separate, narrowly-scoped subagent?

choices.text: Subagents are required any time a tool has real-world side effects.
A narrowly-scoped subagent given only the email tool and explicit approval criteria reduces the chance the main agent sends outreach while reasoning about unrelated research tools.
The main agent's context window is too small to hold the email tool's schema.
Subagents execute faster than tools called directly by the main agent.

questions.explanation: A narrowly-scoped subagent with only the outreach tool and explicit criteria minimizes accidental sends while the main agent reasons about unrelated tools. A overgeneralizes; C and D are unsupported technical claims.

Read only the first 50 rows of every funding-data result.
Delegate the funding-data lookup to a subagent that returns a distilled summary of relevant findings.
Disable funding lookups and rely on `find_contacts` alone.

questions.explanation: Delegating the funding lookup to a subagent that returns a distilled summary keeps the main agent's context focused on prioritization. A and B don't address the root accumulation problem; D removes needed capability.

Just the final error message, since the rep can re-investigate from there.

A structured handoff summary: what was researched, what was found, and a recommended talking point.

questions.prompt: The team wants a hard guarantee that `send_outreach_email` is never called more than once per contact per day, regardless of what the model decides mid-conversation. Question: What is the correct enforcement mechanism?

choices.text: A hook that tracks per-contact call counts/timestamps and blocks the tool call once the daily limit is reached.
A system prompt instruction stating the daily limit clearly.
A note in the tool's description mentioning the limit.
Few-shot examples showing an agent stopping after one email per contact.

questions.explanation: A per-contact call-count/timestamp hook is the only option that deterministically guarantees the limit; B, C, and D remain probabilistic prompt-level guidance.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Cost/Latency Tuning for a Code-Review Assistant
questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: Most PRs are small and the review task is straightforward; latency and cost per PR matter far more than handling rare, deeply architectural changes well. Question: Which model tier best fits the default path?

choices.text: The highest-capability tier available, to guarantee quality on every PR.
A fast, low-latency tier suited to high-volume/low-complexity review, reserving a higher tier only for PRs flagged as complex.
Whichever tier is cheapest per token regardless of task fit.
The same tier used for the company's hardest reasoning tasks, for consistency.

questions.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity tasks fit a fast, low-latency tier, with a higher tier reserved for flagged complex cases — matching capability to actual task difficulty. A and D overspend by default; C ignores task fit.

questions.prompt: A small fraction of PRs require deep multi-file reasoning (a cross-service refactor) where the fast default model produces shallow comments. Question: What is the most targeted fix?

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to the fast model's prompt for every PR.
Switch every PR to the highest-capability tier to be safe.
Increase `max_tokens` for all PRs.
Route only the flagged complex PRs to a higher-capability tier or one with extended/adaptive thinking enabled, keeping the fast path for everything else.

questions.explanation: Targeted routing of only the flagged complex PRs to a higher tier addresses the actual gap without overspending on the high-volume simple path. A, B, and C apply broad, costly fixes to a narrow problem.

questions.prompt: The service currently floats to "whatever model is latest" in production. After a routine model update, review tone and comment structure shifted noticeably without any code change. Question: What should the team do differently?

choices.text: Nothing — behavior drift across releases is expected and requires no process.
Roll back to the oldest available model version permanently.
Disable all prompt caching to prevent drift.
Pin a specific model version in production and deliberately test before upgrading, rather than always floating to latest.

questions.explanation: Pinning and deliberately testing before upgrading avoids unattributed behavior drift in production. A accepts avoidable risk; B and C are unhelpful overcorrections unrelated to the actual fix.

Lower the temperature to zero.
Provide 2–3 few-shot examples demonstrating the exact desired structure.
Ask the model to restate the structure before reviewing.

questions.explanation: Concrete few-shot examples are the most effective lever for consistent structure when prose alone hasn't worked. A repeats a failed approach; B and D don't reliably fix structural consistency.

None — input and output tokens are budgeted completely independently.
Output length has no effect on latency.
Long outputs are always truncated regardless of context window size.

questions.explanation: Input and output share one context-window budget, so a long diff directly constrains available review length and vice versa. B, C, and D misstate this relationship.

Stable, role-defining instructions belong in the system prompt or placed first so they form a consistent, cacheable prefix; diff-specific content should come after as the varying part.

questions.explanation: Stable instructions first (ideally cacheable) and variable content after both improve consistency (clear role separation) and caching. A, B, and D misstate the effect of ordering.

Actual token usage per request — input, output, and cache — attributed per PR, rather than an estimate from average size.
A flat cost assumption based on lines-changed count.

questions.explanation: Actual per-request token usage (input/output/cache) attributed per PR gives an accurate cost picture; estimates from average size or unrelated proxies (A, B, D) don't.

choices.text: The model is broken and producing wrong answers.

LLM output is non-deterministic across calls; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool — evals should tolerate reasonable variation (e.g., checking for required content/structure) rather than asserting exact text.
The eval needs a larger reference string.
Temperature should be increased to fix the intermittent failures.

questions.explanation: LLM output is inherently non-deterministic; exact-string-match evals are the wrong tool and will fail intermittently even on correct output. A and D misdiagnose the cause; C doesn't address the underlying non-determinism.

Summarize the metadata with a second Claude call before reviewing.

Put a brief overview or key-facts summary at the start of the input and organize the detailed content under clear section headers, mitigating the tendency to attend most to the beginning and end of long inputs.

questions.explanation: Placing a key-facts summary up front and organizing detail under clear headers directly counteracts the tendency to under-attend to the middle of long inputs. A is costly and doesn't guarantee the effect disappears; B and C don't address the underlying attention pattern.

questions.scenario_context: Ridgeline DevTools runs a code-review assistant that fires on every pull request across dozens of internal repos, generating inline comments and a review summary. Given the CI volume, cost, latency, and consistency all matter, and the team is tuning model selection, prompting, and context handling to hit targets.
questions.prompt: The review prompt has been modified informally by several engineers over time with no record of what changed or why, making it hard to diagnose a recent quality regression. Question: What practice would have prevented this?

choices.text: Treating prompts as versioned artifacts, similar to code, so changes are tracked and regressions can be attributed and rolled back.
Locking the prompt so no one can ever change it again.
Only allowing one designated engineer to ever read the prompt.
Rewriting the prompt from scratch every quarter.

questions.explanation: Versioning prompts like code enables attribution and rollback for quality regressions. B, C, and D are impractical overcorrections that don't provide the actual missing capability (change tracking).

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A new engineer clones the team's dbt repository, but Claude Code doesn't apply the team's established SQL style conventions for them, even though a teammate's machine applies them correctly. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The new engineer needs to run `/memory` to activate memory files.
CLAUDE.md requires an explicit `@import` from the project root to take effect at all.
The conventions live only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the teammate's machine — user-level config that never travels through version control.
The conventions file exceeded a size limit and was silently truncated.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md never travels through version control, so a new teammate cloning the repo won't see it; team conventions must live in a committed project-level file. A, B, and D misdescribe how CLAUDE.md loading actually works.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to review dbt model changes and consistently hangs until timeout, with no visible error in the logs. Question: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The pull requests are too large for Claude Code to process.
The CI runner lacks permission to call the Claude API.
The job is missing `-p`/`--print` (headless mode), so the process is waiting for interactive input the CI runner never provides.
The repository's CLAUDE.md is malformed.

questions.explanation: Missing headless/non-interactive mode causes the process to wait for input a CI runner never provides, producing a hang rather than a clean error. A, B, and D would typically produce different, more specific failure signatures.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A downstream service parses Claude Code's pipeline-review output with regex to post inline comments on dbt pull requests, and the parser breaks whenever output formatting drifts slightly between runs. Question: What is the robust fix?

choices.text: Harden the regex with more permissive fallback patterns.
Run with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` defining the findings structure for machine-parseable output.
Post the entire raw output as a single PR comment instead of parsing it.
Add a stronger prompt instruction never to deviate from the format.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained JSON output via `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` is machine-parseable by construction, removing the fragile dependency on prose format stability. A, C, and D are reactive or abandon the structured-comment requirement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `/audit-lineage` custom command prints thousands of lines of table-lineage graph data, and engineers report that Claude's answers about their actual task get noticeably worse right after running it. Question: What frontmatter change fixes this?

choices.text: `allowed-tools`, restricting the command to read-only operations.
`argument-hint`, so engineers scope the analysis more narrowly.
`context: fork`, so the command's verbose output runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Removing the command entirely.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` isolates verbose output in a sub-agent context so only a summary returns, directly fixing the described context pollution. A restricts capability, not output destination; B narrows scope but doesn't isolate output; D removes useful functionality.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An internal `/scaffold-pipeline` skill is meant only to create new files from a template, but an audit finds a session where it also ran shell commands that modified unrelated files. Question: What is the correct guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning in the skill's instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, making Bash unavailable during execution.
Require engineers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism that makes Bash structurally unavailable during the skill's execution. A is probabilistic and the violation already happened despite instructions; C mitigates damage rather than preventing it; D is a false claim about slash commands.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An engineer needs to understand how a complex data-lineage flow crosses an unfamiliar warehouse schema before making a change, and worries that reading dozens of model files will exhaust context before implementation begins. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Read every file in the schema in one pass to be thorough.
Skip exploration and infer the schema from table names.
Split the work across two separate terminal windows.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in a separate context, preserving the main conversation's budget for implementation. B floods context directly; C guesses instead of investigating; D doesn't share context between windows meaningfully.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but the engineer still needs to implement the pipeline change in the same session and wants to preserve key findings. Question: What should they do?

choices.text: Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what was learned.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free context space.
Continue working; Claude automatically discards irrelevant context.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free context while preserving key information, the correct mid-session relief valve. B discards findings; C frees trivial space while losing standards; D describes behavior that doesn't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A multi-step Claude Code task that reads a pipeline config, calls the warehouse-query MCP tool, and writes a report produces a wrong final report. Trace logs show the config was read correctly and the MCP tool returned valid data. Question: Where should debugging focus next?

choices.text: Re-read the config file again, since that's the earliest step.

The step between receiving the MCP tool's valid data and producing the final report — since inputs were confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how the model reasoned about or transformed that data afterward.
The network connection to the MCP server, since that's the most complex step.
Nothing — a wrong final report with correct inputs means the task should simply be re-run.

questions.explanation: Since the config and MCP data were both confirmed correct, the divergence is most likely in how that verified-correct data was subsequently reasoned about or transformed — that's where the trace should focus next. A and C re-check already-verified steps; D skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: A pipeline-status tool integration fails, and the team can't tell whether the failure is in their integration code (bad auth, wrong endpoint) or in something the model did. Question: What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Assume it's a model problem and rewrite the prompt.
Isolate whether the failure occurred at the integration layer (the actual API/tool call and its response) versus in the model's output, by examining the trace of exactly what was sent and received.
Switch to a different model to see if the failure persists.
Restart the CI runner and try again.

questions.explanation: Isolating integration-layer versus model-output failure requires examining the actual trace of what was sent and received, before assuming which side is at fault. A and C guess without diagnosis; D doesn't investigate the cause at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The internal warehouse-query capability needs to be reachable from Claude Code sessions across the whole data org, not just one team, and should be maintainable by the platform team independently of any consuming application. Question: What is the best approach?

choices.text: Have each team paste warehouse credentials into their own CLAUDE.md.
Hard-code query logic into each team's custom skill separately.
Build an MCP server exposing warehouse-query operations as tools, shared across the org.
Ask each engineer to run the warehouse CLI manually when needed.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposing shared tools org-wide, maintained centrally, matches the cross-application reuse and independent-maintenance requirement. A, B, and D all fail to provide reusable, centrally maintained access.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An MCP server for the data catalog exposes both a `search_tables` tool and a way for agents to see what tables and schemas exist without an exploratory search call. Question: What is the second capability an example of?

choices.text: An MCP resource — content/catalog visibility distinct from a tool, which performs an action.
An MCP tool, functionally identical to `search_tables`.
A built-in tool provided by the platform automatically.
A Claude Code Skill.

questions.explanation: Visibility into available content without an action call is the defining trait of an MCP resource, distinct from a tool that performs an action. B, C, and D mischaracterize this capability.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team is deciding whether the pipeline-status MCP server should run as a local stdio process per engineer's machine or as a remote, centrally-hosted network service. Question: What should drive the decision?

choices.text: stdio servers are always faster regardless of deployment context.
MCP only supports one communication pattern, so there's no real decision to make.
Where the server needs to run relative to the client and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine/local resources, remote/network hosting for centrally shared services accessed by many clients.
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources.

questions.explanation: The choice should follow where the server needs to run and who needs access — local stdio for per-machine resources, remote hosting for centrally shared services. A, B, and D are false or oversimplified claims about MCP's communication patterns.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repository, currently has a warehouse API token hardcoded directly in the file. Question: What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token before committing it.
Move `.mcp.json` to a private repository instead.
Rotate the token weekly instead of removing it from the file.
Move the token to environment-variable expansion (e.g., `${WAREHOUSE_TOKEN}`) so the secret isn't committed to version control.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret out of the version-controlled file while the file itself remains shareable. A is easily reversible obfuscation, not real protection; B and C don't remove the exposed credential from history or ongoing risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: An audit finds that several MCP-connected tools grant broader access (e.g., full table-drop rights) than any actual data-engineering workflow requires. Question: What is the correct remediation, consistent with least-privilege principles?

choices.text: Add logging so misuse can be reviewed after the fact.
Add a confirmation prompt before any drop operation.
Leave access as-is, since no misuse has been observed yet.
Scope the exposed tools down to only the operations actual workflows require, removing unnecessary broad capabilities rather than just monitoring them.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means removing unnecessary capability, not just observing or slowing its misuse. A and B are detective/compensating controls; C accepts unnecessary risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: MCP Servers for a Data-Engineering Team
questions.scenario_context: Cascade Analytics has a 40-engineer data-engineering team that uses Claude Code alongside internal MCP servers for warehouse queries, pipeline status, and a data catalog. You lead team-wide configuration, CI integration, and troubleshooting.
questions.prompt: The platform team is choosing how to expose a one-off, team-specific data-quality reporting workflow used by a single small team, versus a widely-reused schema-validation capability needed by every pipeline agent across the org. Question: How should each be built?

choices.text: Both as MCP servers, since MCP is the correct choice for any shared capability.

The one-off reporting workflow as a Skill or custom tool scoped to that team; the widely-reused schema-validation capability as an MCP server or built-in tool maintained centrally and shared across all consuming agents.
Both as Skills, since Skills are always reusable.
Both as built-in tools, since built-in tools require the least setup.

questions.explanation: Matching each capability's actual reuse scope — Skill/custom tool for the one-off, team-specific workflow; MCP or built-in tool for the widely shared, centrally maintained capability — is the correct architecture. A, C, and D force every capability into one category regardless of its actual reuse profile. --- *End of Practice Exam 12.*
